subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF ALLEGED INVOLVEMENT IN ILLEGAL REBATES TO DUTCH BUSINESSMAN-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. My motion is prompted by the revelation that a Dutch businessman has been a principal recipient of Polysar rebates to the amount of $3 million. In view of the fact that this could involve a corporation owned by the government of Canada in aiding and abetting criminal activity, contrary to the interests of one of this country's NATO allies, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees):
That this House direct the Prime Minister to call upon the RCMP to investigate the case and give the fullest possible co-operation to the Dutch authorities.

speechtext:

ESTABLISHMENT OF CONSERVATION POLICY AND DEBATE ON NEED FOR MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-MOTION UNDER S.O.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that the chairman of our national energy company, Petro-Canada, last week criticized the government's lack of action on a national energy policy, and referred to it as a process of ad hoc decisions which may well lead us down a path of no return to an energy future for which coming generations may have little to thank us, and in view of the strong leadership shown on this matter by President Carter, after being in office barely four months, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn):
That this government move from ad hoc decision-making in the area of conservation, as well as other aspects of energy policy, to laying out a full and comprehensive policy which would include letting parliament debate on behalf of the people of Canada, whether a pipeline should be built from the Mackenzie Valley.

REQUEST FOR INCREASED QUOTAS AND DELIVERY SPACE IN ELEVATORS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43 I request leave to move a motion to discuss a matter of most urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the tight economic situation in many parts of Saskatchewan brought about by the low final payment, which in many cases amounted to one per cent per bushel; the drought situation in western Canada causing businesses to deny credit, the banks to deny loans on cattle because of depressed prices; and the inability of farmers to deliver grain since boxcars are not being

spotted because of the low protein content of grain in many of the areas, and many elevators not shipping any grain since last November now being told that they will have to wait until the shipping season in Churchill commences some time toward the end of July, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton):
That the Wheat Board immediately increase the quota and provide boxcars and delivery space to elevators in order that farmers may meet their cash requirements for spring seeding and not delay deliveries until it is convenient for the administration but not the farmer.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: ALLEGEDLY ILLEGAL REBATE TO DUTCH BUSINESSMAN-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION AND REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the specific question, there has not been a government to government contact in this regard. What has happened is that over some two months ago the government directors on the Canada Development Corporation communicated to the board of the CDC the Prime Minister's guidelines with respect to conduct of Crown corporations. subsubtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF DOME TO CONTROL BLOWOUT OF WELL IN BEAUFORT SEA-POLICY ON FUTURE DRILLING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of the Environment. It arises from the oil blowout in the North Sea and from the recommendation made by the deputy minister of the Department of the Environment not to renew drilling in the Beaufort Sea during the coming summer. Would the minister confirm that Dome Petroleum lost control of a well in the Beaufort Sea last summer as a direct result of the government reducing its standards for blowout control and, related to that, would the minister confirm that Dome has not yet been able to seal off completely the hole in question?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
subsubtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF DOME TO CONTROL BLOWOUT OF WELL IN BEAUFORT SEA-POLICY ON FUTURE DRILLING
speechtext:
The hon. member is obviously referring to the testimony given to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry by the assistant deputy minister, Mr. Edgeworth, expressing the preference that drilling should be delayed until such time as better engineering techniques are developed, which could be quite a few years down the road. As I said yesterday, these problems have to be weighed against other factors, and this is exactly what we are endeavouring to do before deciding on the renewal of the permit.
As to the matter of reducing standards, I am not familiar with that part of the hon. member's question. Certainly we are looking at imposing additional conditions on drilling, if drilling is to take place, and that will be the subject of our discussions. I am not acquainted with the suggestion that the well is still out of control. That has not been reported to me.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF DOME TO CONTROL BLOWOUT OF WELL IN BEAUFORT SEA-POLICY ON FUTURE DRILLING
speechtext:
For the minister's information, the government did reduce its standards of control last summer and the blowout that occurred was not adequately sealed. That information is available through other government agencies.
I should like to ask the minister, considering that his department has authorized in the past month several million dollars to be spent over a period of time on research into dealing with oil spills specifically in the Arctic, whether he would not agree that the allocation of this large sum of money is an explicit acknowledgement that the technology for control of a blowout once it occurs in the Arctic is not yet adequate, and if he agrees that this is an acknowledgement of it, why is he hesitating in terms of recommending to the government not to proceed with further drilling until we have adequate control techniques?

subsubtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF DOME TO CONTROL BLOWOUT OF WELL IN BEAUFORT SEA-POLICY ON FUTURE DRILLING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the allocation of resources mentioned by the hon. member is in relation to the whole program of exploration and the knowledge and capacity to exercise control if and when drilling does take place. I do not see that program as being only involved in containing oil spills. That is obviously something in which the Minister of Transport, myself and other departments would be involved. I should make clear to the hon. member that our approach to drilling in the north is one of worry and caution and of underlining the dangers involved. There is no way-and I think the hon. member said this yesterday in a television interview-to have an absolutely fool-proof system.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR SIGNING NEW LABOUR CONTRACT THAT WOULD JEOPARDIZE DIRECTOR'S AUTHORITY-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to put a question to the Solicitor General.
Considering that our prison directors have lost a great part of their authority and control over penitentiaries, that some locals of the union of penitentiary employees wield the real control over those institutions through the use of intimidation and violence, and considering that this Parliament has established a sub-committee of 13 members to find solutions to that problem, could the Solicitor General, before the report of the sub-committee is introduced in the House, give us any good reasons for the signature of the new labour contract with the union, for that contract substantially reduces the authority of the director of the institution and therefore officially endorses the anarchy and loss of control we observe in some prisons?
April 26, 1977

subsubtopic: REASON FOR SIGNING NEW LABOUR CONTRACT THAT WOULD JEOPARDIZE DIRECTOR'S AUTHORITY-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if 1 understand the hon. member correctly, he is suggesting that the collective labour contract signed by the Canadian Penitentiary Service and the Public Service Alliance should not have been signed during the parliamentary inquiry. Obviously I cannot support that statement. I am eagerly awaiting the recommendations the parliamentary committee will see fit to submit and I shall be willing to consider them very sympathetically, for that committee has already discussed for long hours and very seriously the problems of the Canadian penitentiary system.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION OF NEW FACILITIES PRIOR TO REPORT OF COMMITTEE
ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION OF NEW FACILITIES PRIOR TO REPORT OF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask a supplementary.
Could the Solicitor General tell the House why he keeps on announcing the building of new penitentiaries in Canada, since the committee has not yet completed its report and will make suggestions about new construction?

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION OF NEW FACILITIES PRIOR TO REPORT OF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it goes without saying that if I announce the building of new penitentiaries in Canada, this is because the inmate population has increased considerably in recent years. We do not choose those who become inmates, they are referred to us by the courts after their cases have been considered. Concerning the parliamentary committee's recommendations, it goes again without saying, Mr. Speaker, that when I announce a new penitentiary will be built on a particular site, from a timing viewpoint it does not prevent me at all from mentioning and taking into consideration the practical recommendations made to me by the committee looking into the penitentiary issue, which is expected to report to me on May 13. At that time, I will obviously be able to take into consideration the construction of penitentiaries.

subsubtopic: THREATENING OF CBC CAMERA CREW OUTSIDE URBAN CONSULATE-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Solicitor General can report briefly to the House on the incident which took place in Montreal in which a security man outside the Cuban consulate threatened a CBC camera crew with a gun while the crew was trying to elicit some information in a background way concerning many things with regard to Cuba as well as the disappearance of the Canadian journalist, Douglas Newby, in Angola.

subsubtopic: THREATENING OF CBC CAMERA CREW OUTSIDE URBAN CONSULATE-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 22 last I understand that two CBC employees were challenged by a Barnes security guard as they began to photograph the Cuban consulate in Montreal. As 1 understand
Oral Questions
it, the Barnes security guard at the consulate was under contract with the Department of External Affairs. The hon. member raised the question as to why they were carrying guns. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a supplementary question to the Acting Prime Minister about the matter of the missing Canadian journalist, Douglas Newby, which concerned the CBC at the time. Their letter of June 16, 1976 says that there is a Cuban embassy in Kinshasa, but they would not be in a position to be of any help to us. In view of the longstanding nature of this affair involving the disappearance of Mr. Newby, I wonder if the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs has discovered why Cuba, which was so important and prominently involved in Angola, was not able to help us. subsubtopic: INQUIRY IF DEPARTMENT PLANS TO ESTABLISH OWN SECURITY SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Minister of National Revenue.
Last Saturday we read in a news release put out by the taxation section of her department that the minister wants to have her own security service branch. Naturally this would mean increasing the staff of the department. Can she tell the House whether that is really her intention and whether she has accepted the recommendation of her officials to organize her own security system, or whether she has consulted her colleague, the Minister of Supply and Services; and tell us why there has been dissatisfaction within her department with regard to the services given for years? In addition, can she say whether the level of salaries paid is a consideration, and whether she is willing to see her staff increased by 50 employees or more merely to ensure the security of files during the night and over weekends?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY IF DEPARTMENT PLANS TO ESTABLISH OWN SECURITY SYSTEM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as minister I recently signed the next estimates of my department and I do not recall having signed anything to increase, by fifty employees, our security staff. The House resumed, from Monday, April 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-20, respecting the office of the Auditor General of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday in that portion of the debate which was alloted to me under this stage of Bill C-20 I indicated that parliament had lost one of the effective means of control over the administration. It was not yesterday, it was not the day before; it goes back over ten years. I refer to the loss of control over supply. I remember very well that a government fell in 1963 on the basis of non-adoption of a motion with regard to interim supply. Various political pundits of more ancient or very junior vintage have lost sight of this fact. Political scientists inveigh against the lack of control by parliament over government.
What hurts me more is that we have members of this House of more respectable vintage and of more junior status who talk about the irrelevance of the known value of this place. They give credence to what I think are purely uninformed, ignorant attributes of what is a parliamentary system. Far too many people feel that this House should be some sort of quasi-
Auditor General Act
administrative body, much like some village councils seem to feel that they are not only going to decide policy but they are going to issue the building permits. This is not the place for that, nor is it the place for assessment of the performance of this chamber based upon the question period.
The efficacy of ministers should not be assessed on how they answer questions, and I say this deliberately as a member of the opposition. I have been on the government side, and I have been Speaker of the House, with some knowledge of the administrative responsibilities of ministers and of their House performance. Some ministers who are supposedly undistinguished as performers in that daily bullring or bearpit that we have are very efficient ministers from an administrative point of view. Certain members of the opposition as well as government members who, in the eyes of commentators, are great people, frankly do not know which end they are coming out of because they make a lot of noise and they are totally irrelevant. But that does not seem to bother anybody as long as they make a lot of noise and they fan the breeze.
Wherein lies the control of the government, if not within parliament? Parliament is a deliberative chamber, not administrative. It sets the policies. But all too often-and I come back to the other point-far too many city aldermen, village councillors and people in general say that elected officials shall be the administrators, that they shall issue the dog licences, they shall issue the building permits, they shall issue goodness knows what. This does not belong to them. It does not belong to the House to determine which permit DREE shall issues. The policy with regard to DREE shall be determined as a result of debate, and if it takes ten days, it shall take ten days. If it takes only one day to set it, fine. But this is not an administrative chamber.
I find, after a great number of years of experience in the House, that there is a total misconception of what parliament shall be. It boils down to this very bill. The Auditor General is the watchdog over the spending practices of government. He is the one who shall report to this deliberative and final body for approval. After all, this chamber is charged with the passsage of the estimates which are the spending programs of the government, the proposals of the government in carrying out its policies.
The report of the Auditor General says in effect, "Yes, your proposals were such, but this was your performance", and it asks that the representatives of the people judge the government on the basis of its performance. It has been years- it almost goes back into antiquity- that the peccadillos laid out in a certain part of the Auditor General's report have drawn the greatest of public comment in the media. Frankly, they are running after little squirrels and mice when they do that. But it is popular. This ministry did this, and that ministry did that. I say this, Mr. Speaker: hindsight is a cheap commodity. It is the cheapest commodity on the market today, and the opinions, based upon hindsight, have equal value with the value on the market. But the review must exist.

April 26, 1977
Auditor General Act
I want to come around to what facilities membrs of parliament, particularly on the government side, have brought to assess government performance. Is there to be a simple slave following? Because ministers say yea on any given subject, even the state of the weather or the state of their own digestion, are the backbenchers to say, in unison yea? Is it to be that notwithstanding what the government says, the opposition reaction shall be merely a knee jerk to the contrary? I do not agree with that. No side of the House has a monopoly on intelligence. Whether or not the government is backed by administration, in my experience from both sides of the House the government has been served, not only by brains but by dunces when it comes to judging political acceptability and I shall say in French-
"la rentabilite de certaines politiques".
There is no way that the government can arrogate unto itself all that wisdom. But listening to government committee members it was as though it was Ascension Sunday every time a minister made a pronouncement with regard to government legislation. It seems as though the tongues of fire of wisdom had descended upon the minister or his parliamentary secretary and senior officials in so far as government supporters are concerned, that is, with some salutary exceptions. The opposition is driven into a knee-jerk syndrome, as I have said, with regard to many proposals that come forward merely because of the attitude of government supporters. There is good legislation that comes forward, perhaps not entirely in all degrees, but basically in principle.
Surely to goodness there is room for disagreement, even within parties, without being charged by unshaven young commentators that there are deep splits in political parties. We are people representing various regions of the country with different emphases and different views. If it were a simple procedure to have but one unqualified and unanimous voice to be heard in this chamber, we would have the Prime Minister on one side and the Leader of the Opposition on the other. They would either agree or disagree. However, in the Cartesian philosophy of the Prime Minister, if there is disagreement, even as to five degrees, it is total disagreement: if we do not agree with the Prime Minister, then we must disagree with him. Nonsense! There can be disagreement as to degree or variation, but often there is agreement in principle and there is no such thing as total confrontation. That is the philosophy of fools. If in this House we were to get the advocacy of one voice on one side and one voice on the other it would be a matter of confrontation and then divide. That is the most foolish philosophy for Canadians in a federation composed as this one is ever to adopt.
How do we get from this philosophy to the present bill? The bill says that the Auditor General shall discharge certain specific tasks. As a result of a report by the independent review board with regard to the Auditor General, the minister

did a volte-face on Mr. Macdonell's recommendation about the appointment of a comptroller general. There has been a change in the philosophy at the head of Treasury Board. Goodness only knows that we have seen such changes before. I recall when the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Drury) was president of the treasury board. There were certain things various members on the government and opposition sides advanced with regard to pensions of former public servants, armed services personnel, RCMP and members of the House of Commons. The then minister absolutely shut his mind to these views.
The hon. member for Westmount was succeeded by the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) and there was a total change. The recommendations of the present Auditor General with regard to a comptroller general were made to the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The attitude of the government, immediately Pavlovian, led it to reject that proposal.
However, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) has looked at the situation somewhat differently-and perhaps his officials have also had a second look at it-and the reaction has not been so Pavlovian. I am looking at page 28-6 of the estimates which is headed "Treasury Board, Central Administration of the Public Service Program". The objectives are laid out. There is a program description which includes expenditure management. Frankly, all the minister has proposed is that there shall be a comptroller general with the rank of deputy minister. Yesterday I referred to arbitrary strictures of the government as to where this man shall sit in the pecking order of the super-mandarins, to use a polite term. This man is to look after expenditure management. I will read into the record what this says:
On the basis of the analysis of departmental plans and programs to recommend to the government the acceptance or modification of specific expenditure proposals in order to:
-reflect the priorities which the government assigns to the objectives;
-increase the effectiveness of existing and proposed programs;
-increase the efficiency with which the manpower, facilities, equipment, materials and supplies are used in the operation of programs; and to -develop the estimates for the approval of parliament.
That, effectively, is going to be the job of the comptroller general. There is one point with regard to Treasury Board on which, since parliament has lost control over the determination of the estimates, I will join with my colleague, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), in saying that as far as the Canadian public is concerned, the only control over government which is left is public scrutiny. Public scrutiny was really endemic to the examination and control of estimates. If reasons could not be established, or if expenditures could not be justified, then government was to be held in suspense: it was to be held responsible. This is the purpose of parliament. I consider it a shallow political science that the effectiveness of this chamber should be based on the yards of bills or inches of pages of legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members for allowing me to continue my remarks. I shall be brief. I now come to the conclusion of my proposals. The effectiveness of this chamber is not measured by yards of legislation or by the thickness of statutes. The government may propose omnibus bills; it may propose yards of bills; it may propose scores of bills. Anyone looking at the order paper might say that the government has placed there "X" dozen bills, but parliament has dealt with only a few. That attitude is wrong, because parliament may have faced nothing but trivia, absolute garbage, or the ultimate in drivel in the consideration of essential bills on which parliament must take a stand.
However, let it not be said that stands are taken on the opposition side only. In case ministers of the Crown are not aware of it, and in case the absent press and media are not aware of this, many government backbenchers sit back in committee and question the wisdom of certain legislation. They are conscientious legislators, doing their work quietly and effectively. Such parliamentarians are found on both sides of the House. But they will not get the garlands of the headlines. Good gracious me, that would be too banal for the press. In order to get attention they would have to stand in this chamber and do a strip-dance. It is said that in a military campaign the generals get the glory, but the soldiers fighting in the trenches do the dirty work. No truer aphorism could be applied to this House.
Certain members opposite on the government side, some beside me in the opposition, and some so-called star members of this House, say that the committee system is a joke, that we should improve it. Almost any hon. member could make suggestions for improvement. If one said that our committee system could not be improved, one would be, frankly, derelict in one's duty, because nothing is perfect. I know that I have many allies on the government side for my views about improving the efficacy of this chamber and the committees. Mr. Speaker, such institutions are not sausage machines for the production of legislation: they are places for the examination and deliberation of policies put forward.
This is a chamber of debate. It is not a pseudo-administrative tribunal. As I say, it is a deliberative chamber, a chamber for the expression of points of view on the part of people from various parts of the country. If they do not accord with Toronto, damn Toronto. If they do not accord with Montreal, damn Montreal. Members here represent their parts of the country. If their views do not suit Vancouver, damn Vancouver. Damn Edmonton, too.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Did you say Edmonton, too?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Yes. This is the place where we express the points of view representative of our
Auditor General Act
people. If we are stupid enough a couple of years from now to increase the membership of this House to 284 members, it will mean we will have another 18 members clamouring to express their opinions. Then shall government backbenchers, the press, or the opposition gainsay the opportunity for those new members to express their views? Shall they be foreclosed from expressing their opinions because that would extend debate? Such ideas are nonsense. There is no way one can put a lid on a deliberative chamber.
Newspaper editors love to take positions. Newspaper correspondents set up their stories. I am not attacking any of them personally, Mr. Speaker. Such criticism is one of the hazards of their trade. They have stories to set up, lead paragraphs to write and conclusions to reach. The next day they will not deny their first conclusions, even though the debate may have turned around 180 degrees, even though the direction of the debate on its second day may be completely opposite to the direction on its first day.
Editorial writers pronounce themselves-I do not know on what basis-and thereafter any extension of debate is a nuisance: it is pronounced to be a filibuster; it is tiresome. After all, they have expressed themselves. I sometimes wish that this House could be entirely composed of newspaper editors and academics. We would see the greatest viewing with alarm, the greatest performance from the highest of ivory towers. Oh, yes, they serve a function, without doubt. But colleagues opposite, and on this side-and I have been on both sides of the House-respond to editorials and newspaper columns like quail do to the first blast of a shotgun. They run. They do not look at things calmly, nor assess them from one end of the country to another.
Why should members of parliament have better facilities? Let me read from a Treasury Board declaration on the central administration of the public service program, for my point ties right in with what we are saying about the Auditor General. What are the objectives of the program? They involve:
Evaluation and planning-development and application of methods and procedures for:
-evaluating the effectiveness and efficiency of programs and projects, and
-ensuring that the government has the information it requires to make and
carry out decisions to increase program effectiveness and operating efficiency.
That is precisely what members of parliament require. The words "evaluating the effectiveness and efficiency of programs and projects" are the alpha and omega of the study of the estimates. Such evaluation applies not only to the opposition; it applies also to government backbenchers. I sat as one for many years. They are as much in the dark about government programs as anybody else. How can they assume, except out of party loyalty, that the government is correct? Remember, the government is very much separated from its backbenchers because it depends entirely on the advice of the administration. The opposition has its own limited research facilities.

Seeing that there are four government backbenchers in the House at the present time, all I can say is that they take for gospel any legislation that is flashed before them. They are the greatest victims of subliminal advertising put before them by cabinet. As my colleague has said, they are subject to mass hypnotism when anything is proposed by government. Yet, Mr. Speaker, here lies the effective means for them to join other members of parliament. I am not going to say what recourse the government has in obtaining information; perhaps it has certain privileges. When I was a member of cabinet there were, I think, 22 members. The cabinet has now grown to over 30 members. It is getting to the point where it exceeds its power regarding both its own supporters and the opposition. Both sides of the House should be equal. Mr. Speaker, you in your individual capacity as a member have equal status, in terms of acquiring information, with any member on the government side, whether his chair is occupied or not, or any member sitting to my left, whether his chair is occupied or not.
In so far as the government and the Canadian people are concerned, it is high time we obtained this information. I would hope that in putting this legislation into effect the minister would indicate that a great deal more information will be coming out of Treasury Board than hitherto, and that there will be, in so far as Crown corporations are concerned, a lifting of the veil by government undertaking.

This committee should be established without debate. This would give parliament a greater degree of control over the affairs of this nation. Individual backbenchers must weigh this consideration. If, along the way, either by carelessness or slavishness, we abandon that charge, there is a derogation of duty. I do not intend to be one of those who shall be labelled as either derogating his duties or slavishly following a bad custom. I demand much more information. This is after 20 years in this House. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, everyone should be concerned with the changes that we have made in the rules and the fact that we have not now, in my opinion, any idea of the expenditures made by the federal government. If you look at the blue book of expenditures, you will be as confused as members have been since those changes have taken place as to what actually are the expenditures. Therefore, I am very pleased to support this piece of legislation. We have changed the rules until we are out of the ball game as far as financial control is concerned. If we can strengthen the Auditor General to make him more effective on our behalf, we had certainly better do so. The establishment of the new officer to assist us in financial control seems to be a step in the right direction.
One of the functions of a democratic parliament is that members of parliament have the right to question the expenditures of the government. There has never been a government less interested in what members of parliament do about expenditures than this government. All they have to do is drag their feet in committees. There were many who thought we could handle the expenditures of the nation more efficiently if we were to discuss them in committee rather than in the House. If the responsible ministers do not want to come to the commit-
Auditor General Act
tee, they do not come. Seldom a minister ever comes more than two or three times to the whole committee hearing. He leaves the other discussions to his officials.
The thing you hear most often in discussing the estimates is that that is a policy matter and is beyond their jurisdiction. Either those public servants work for us as a parliament, or they work directly for the minister and they are responsible to the minister. If they are only responsible to the minister, for goodness sake do not come to the committee, because they really cannot tell us anything unless we want to carry on a university education in some particular subject.
We are interested in policy decisions. We are interested in whether this item is passed and whether it becomes an expenditure in fact, or whether the expenditure was for something else. An indication of where members of parliament are not competent to deal with expenditures is the 64 SI items introduced this year-statutory items. The $1 item does not mean anything. It is only an entry in the book of estimates. It may mean something, or it may mean nothing. Under the statutory $1 item the government can spend millions of dollars and can embark upon totally new programs and institute almost any departmental change that it wishes-all on the strength of a $1 item which the minister does not have to explain and which, obviously, does not say what it is meant to say.
Years ago, in my opinion, we knew at the end of a session, when we came to discussing the estimates, that those estimates had to be passed, hopefully, while they were still estimates rather than public accounts. We were able to find a place where the backbencher or the individual member of parliament was able to stand up and take out the item he wished to speak on and make his point, because the detail was there and the information was provided. He could make that point very forcefully. If he was not satisfied in his questioning of the minister, and if he did not receive full information, he could hold up the estimate until the minister was very upset and concerned and was willing to make full disclosure. This is not possible now with any departmental estimate.
Maybe there has to be a change. We always look to the British system. Not long ago I visited England with a committee. There were two things that surprised me. There is absolutely no democracy in the operation of the British parliament as we know it. It is machined, engineered, set up and probably agreed to by most people. If it is not agreed to, there is nothing anyone can do about it. I was interested to know what is done with third parties in England. The whip of the governing party stated that they just ignore them; they do not take them into consideration. If they want an election, that is what they get. They do not take them into consideration in terms of estimates, either.
Around the end of May all the estimates will come back to the House. One night they will come to an end. When the estimates are called, the only thing a member of parliament can do is object and call for a vote. The government majority, without the members on the government side knowing what it

I find that the same complaints were made by the auditor general in the late 1800s. The auditor general of the day-1893-John Lorn McDougall, stated:
I have failed again to obtain either adequate staff for my office or even a modicum of co-operation.
That is the complaint I have heard of the Auditor General ever since coming here. I will probably continue to hear it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Not with this bill. He has full authority.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
He is being given a workload that will replace members of parliament. He will have to do what members of parliament were elected to do in so far as expenditures are concerned. He will have to be given a very competent staff which will have to work very hard. They will review all expenditures and make recommendations. They will find difficulty in getting information from some departments. They will not only have the opportunity of doing the job they have had to do in terms of the government, but they will have to make some investigation into Crown corporations. They will have to ask for the co-operation of Crown corporations which are not even audited by the Auditor General's department. This is a first. The minister is to be given full credit. I appreciate the fact that the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) is now on the government side. The government was previously opposed to this, and now they are willing. Possibly he should get some of the credit.
The second addition is the establishment of the office of comptroller general. Members of parliament will take his report and make a judgment on it in terms of whether we agree with what has been done with regard to the operation of the various programs he examines.
Maybe it is necessary for members of parliament to have a bureaucracy. Maybe it is necessary for us to have research people. Maybe we should get involved with exchanging paper with one department and another, as well as exchanges between our research people and other research people, the comptroller general and the Auditor General, and the Auditor General and various departments such as Treasury Board and Supply and Services. Maybe exchanging paper would be a good thing. However, it is no substitute for making available sufficient information with regard to expenditures in the blue book in order to enable an individual member of parliament who is concerned about a specific problem to look and see what, exactly, an expenditure is for.
Possibly parliament has grown too much. We may have gone ahead too fast. If so, we will have to change our system and our thinking about the system. Instead of electing members of parliament to supervise government expenditures, we will be elected to supervise the auditor general, the comptroller general and, I hope, another officer of the House, the "expenditure general."
In the United States they set forth what they are going to accomplish in a particular program, its cost, its efficiency and whether they are getting their money's worth. If we operated that system in Canada, we would find out some very interesting things. We would find out that we are making expenditures on programs that are not efficient. I would like to deal with one example, DREE. When DREE was originally introduced, it was seen as a solution to the problems of the underdeveloped areas. It was going to provide them with the know-how and assistance to develop their resources in a most efficient way. We believed it would bring about decentralization of production in this nation.
I was particularly interested because I come from an area of primary development, namely an area of mining and forest industries. In Kirkland Lake there was a very large infrastructure, including churches, schools, roads, and everything else necessary for a modern town. When the mines were depleted the people were unable to find employment in order to maintain that infrastucture: they had a great deal of difficulty.
1 agree that DREE has been of some assistance. However, if we had an "expenditures general" to look into some of these DREE projects he would come to a very sad conclusion. A newspaper report the other day indicated that in the Renfrew area 50 per cent of DREE projects went bankrupt. Many of those projects have received two DREE grants. An "expenditures general" would see that that is very bad business. Why give to the same company, in the same enterprise, in the same community, the same grant twice? An "expenditures general" would say whether there should be that input in the first place, and whether there should be a grant in the second instance. There would be no necessity for it going bankrupt and causing the bankruptcy of the man supplying the few trucks, and the local businessman supplying the welding unit, the businessman who had advance credit for whatever services had to be provided. He would not have been hit twice.
That is the major tragedy in every community where a business goes bankrupt. It is not only the business that goes bankrupt, but all the services of the community which, of necessity, have to carry 30 days' credit with that industry. I am sure that an "expenditures general" would say that we must have equity for any money we advance to that business. In my area there are now four bankruptcies. Three of the companies have been assisted by DREE. Let us take an example of a sawmill in my area, a fairly large one. Some money was put into it under DREE and it went into operation. Later it went bankrupt. Then we put some more money into the company, and again it went bankrupt. If we had had equity in that plant-say we put up 25 per cent of the capital-we would have had some say on the board of directors and some say in how that plant was run.

April 26, 1977

I am sure changes would have been made, because it is reported that the management may have bought a race horse or a motel, or that one of the directors bought a $150,000 home in Toronto or has made other expenditures that any other legitimate director on a board would not have thought of doing, and the money for that would not have come from company funds. If the company needed more money, we could put more money in it and we would, again, take equity and, if necessary, bring Venturetec or one of the other Crown corporations, into partnership to provide managerial assistance.
We have all these people in DREE who have knowledge of industry, and all the people in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce who are highly skilled in industrial development and management. In many cases local businessmen do not have expertise in raising and handling money, nor do they have sales ability. The government can assist them in these areas. If we had equity in those companies, we would be able to do a lot better than we have under DREE. This should be no favour to anyone. I hear that in Cape Breton Island a $1 million make-work project is to be started. I am also told that there will be a new program in two months' time, and another one in the fall, and that we will continually keep people off the unemployment rolls by providing short-term, make-work projects.
If we put in the $1 million, and the money that $1 million will raise, into the steel plant in that area, we could probably have a viable industry employing 400 or 500 people permanently, not temporarily. This would be a partnership between the federal government and the plant. Many of our expenditures are wasted. It seems to me that an "expenditures general" would be able to point that out, and members of parliament who are not stupid but who are badly misinformed would, of necessity, have to make a decision with regard to the program, either to remove it, to improve it or to do something about it, if that information were made available to them.
The final function of the "expenditures general" would be to relate to parliament the cost of the exemptions we grant in our tax structure. Not long ago we had the income tax bill before us. It was interesting to note that if tax credits were indicated, members of parliament would be better able to assess whether or not rapid depreciation-which means that taxpayers are allowed tax exemptions-produced the kinds of results we wished. I am thinking in particular of the studies done by the government examining tax exemptions which were given to industry, the sole purpose of which was to provide employment. In fact, in most cases it enabled the company to provide better equipment, but it reduced the number of people working for that company. The government knows exactly what those exemptions did in terms of providing employment, and it knows how much those exemptions cost the taxpayers, because if you do not get it one way you must get it another. You have to raise a certain amount of money, and if you do not get it from one class of taxpayer because they have an exemption, you get it from someone else.
If you are giving a certain class of taxpayer an exemption, you are putting the burden on everyone else. The government
Auditor General Act
knows the results of that program set up by a previous minister of finance. It is not about to tell you and I, Mr. Speaker, the results of the studies it has carried out, because the government is going to use the same gimmick, with exactly the same result. The result is that other taxpayers will have to raise money for taxpayers who are enjoying an exemption at the expense of all of us.
It is very difficult to convince the government to do anything. They certainly do not want to change, and the reason for that is very simple. Cabinet ministers are like the rest of us: they have only 24 hours a day, which can easily be filled with doing the paperwork with which their departments supply them. If I read the other half of the contents of the garbage can every day, it would take me an extra two hours. I get a full garbage can of stuff from the departments. If that is what I get, the minister must be getting six or seven garbage cans full of stuff which he has no time to read.

speechtext: It depends on the size of the garbage cans.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
You get big ones and little ones. Mine is quite small. The minister is not able to make all the decisions himself. He is provided with information which is all from one point of view. If he had an "expenditures general", he would be able to assess the programs and know whether they were good.
It was interesting to note that in the election campaign south of the border the former governor of Georgia, now President Carter, claimed to have covered the expenditures of all the ancillary services of government only when they proved how valuable they were and provided that kind of information to him and to the legislature. That is not done in this country. If any money is left over after the expenditure is made, there is a hell of a rush to spend it at the end of the year so the government can go ahead and ask for the same amount the next year.
There really has been no possibility of establishing whether we as taxpayers have received value. However, I suggest that this minister has been surprisingly amenable; he has done what the Auditor General has asked. I am sure he will be willing to provide the wherewithal to make it possible for the Auditor General to make the necessary investigations, because parliament is no longer able to make those investigations. Never once has a major expenditure blooper been raised in this House. These have always followed reports of the Auditor General, with the limited capacity he said he had in previous years. That has not been done since the days of having the horses on the payroll. It has not been done by members of parliament. I am not sure how it was done, but that was before my time.
The minister is also to be congratulated for appointing a comptroller general. I hope this will mean there will be a balance between the operations of one department and another. If it had been possible to have a comptroller general previously, we might not have had to get rid of Information

April 26, 1977
Auditor General Act
Canada; we might have been able to put information from every department into Information Canada. That probably would have been a more efficient way of handling it. But what did we do? We set up a new department, and everybody else was running it. There were 28 "information Canada's" in 28 departments, with Information Canada operating as a storefront operation downtown, turning out the same information as the other 28 departments.
I suggest that the minister has gone a long way, and I congratulate him for that, but I hope he will give consideration to appointing an "expenditures general" so we can have an assessment of what expenditures we are making through tax exemptions and we will know the value of the expenditures we are making in Crown corporations. I presume we would not have to be involved with trying to find out, after the fact, who is getting bribes from what Crown corporation or from what department. That kind of foolishness would be stopped. If we were to appoint an "expenditures general", the government would benefit because it would be assured that any program embarked upon would be financially sound and would accomplish what it was supposed to accomplish in terms of return. With an "expenditures general" we would know how much exemptions, whether they be personal or corporate exemptions, would cost taxpayers, and we as members of parliament would be able to judge the effects of that type of expenditure.
I believe we are no longer able to handle expenditures in the way we are presently trying to handle them. I think everyone feels immense frustration. I have felt anger, and stronger feelings than that, when we have had to pass estimates in the House because of deadlines and when no discussion has taken place.
I congratulate the minister for the steps he has taken. I hope he will continue along that line and that I will be in parliament four or five years from now when we will have an "expenditures general" who will be looking at the hundreds of programs we will have and telling us what we are receiving in dollars and cents as a result of the tax expenditures on those programs.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with much of what the hon. member said, particularly about information services, but I wonder if he would like to correct an impression which he inadvertently may have left. Understanding, as 1 do, that Information Canada rarely produced any information itself but, rather, provided centres for the collection and distribution of information produced by others as a convenience to the public, does the hon. member know of situations where Information Canada produced the same kind of information as did the proliferating departmental information sections, or would he not want to correct that impression?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I did not leave that impression. The point I was trying to make was that I was under the impression-and so were many other members of parliament, I am sure-that when we established Information

Canada the idea was that it would be our information-producing agency and that that would eliminate the need for printing units in every other department. However, that is not what happened. It did not get to the stage of producing the documents which were being produced by the departments. The departments continued to do that. They sent it to Information Canada, and Information Canada made it available to the public.
The point I was making was that it would have been more efficient if Information Canada had been doing the printing and the gathering of all the information from the various departments. The departments really continue to propagandize Information Canada instead of propagandizing the general public. I believe Information Canada never really got to the point of being efficient, but we were told to get rid of Information Canada, in my opinion for the wrong reasons.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as vice-chairman of the public accounts committee I am very pleased to join briefly in this debate at second reading of a very important piece of legislation. I am sure those of us in the public accounts committee will be wanting to give a great deal more detailed attention to the bill when it comes before us for clause by clause examination.
I would like to join hon. members on this side and hon. members opposite in commending the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) and the government for bringing forward legislation of this kind at this time, together with the concurrent indication of the appointment of a comptroller general within the public service. I say this because I think we are living at a time when increasing cynicism is being demonstrated by some citizens in this country, by people connected with the media and by others as to the general place of our parliamentary process in their lives and in the lives of ordinary people. I think this bill and the concurrent appointment of the position of comptroller general is an indication of the responsiveness of parliament to an area of concern which obviously touches on the pocketbooks, as it were, of the taxpayers of Canada.
After all, the taxpayers are the people who are responsible for footing the bill for whatever is done under the direction of government at all levels across Canada. I think this Auditor General bill addresses itself to a very real area of concern when, after all, we bear in mind that 10 or 15 years ago the rate of government expenditures at the federal and provincial levels was much less than it is today.
For the first time we are looking at legislation which will govern the responsibilities of our Auditor General. I understand that this kind of position has been in existence for close to 100 years, but until now the authority for the position of Auditor General has really come through the Financial Administration Act, which is an act designed to cover the ground rules for financial administration generally within government as well as the audit of public accounts and financial control of Crown corporations. However, bearing in mind the tremendous size of our budget at the present time and the real need for a completely independent examination of what is
April 26, 1977

happening to expenditures year by year, I think it is very important that the office of the Auditor General be governed by its own act of parliament, and that is what we are doing in this process at the present time.
In the past, the responsibilities of the Auditor General have been defined in terms of the examinations he should make and how he should report. There really has been very little change in the over-all concept of his office in the last 40 years. One appreciates that 40 years ago the Auditor General's job in auditing the books of the government of Canada and its Crown agencies was minuscule compared with the task of the present Auditor General. The whole concept of his investigation has been brought much more sharply into focus in the last ten years as a result of large increases in the budget. These days his job entails examination of the annual spending, by a large organization, of some $44 billion.
The Auditor General himself indicated in committee this morning that in his view this bill is a leader in its field. By introducing this legislation, Canada is setting an example. We are not following the example of some other country, as we have done from time to time. Cynical observers suggest that we tend to follow precedents set elsewhere. In this case we are a leader. Last week, the official from the United Kingdom who holds the position equivalent to our Auditor General expressed intense interest in the bill now before the House for second reading.
Let me make a point to show that parliament responds to suggestions. This bill is the direct result of the recommendations made by the independent review committee which was appointed by the government four years ago and reported two years ago. The independent committee examined this question and made recommendations, and the government has come forward with a bill incorporating many of those recommendations. It must be noted that the Auditor General and members of that independent review committee who examined the bill have indicated their complete satisfaction with the bill and the government's aims. I mention this to show how responsive parliament is to recommendations and studies which the government itself commissioned in the public interest.
This bill is an example of forward-thinking on the part of the government, and I am sure members of parliament will find little difficulty in accepting its general provisions. However, I am concerned about several of its provisions, and I wish to touch on one of those. Basically, the bill addresses itself to the administrative difficulties which the office of the Auditor General has encountered in the past. Many issues have been raised in questioning and controversy has surrounded this area of administration. The bill addresses itself to this particular aspect of the matter. The bill deals with the scope of the audit and the freedom of the Auditor General to report on areas which may legitimately be investigated; that is to say, he may look into those matters with respect to which he feels a report to parliament would be worth while. Basically, therefore, we
Auditor General Act
are considering the independence of the office and the scope of the audit.
The President of the Treasury Board reviewed in his speech some matters concerning the independence of the office of the Auditor General. He indicated, for example, that there are to be selection standards. The office staff are to be appointed by the Auditor General and are not to be subject to Public Service Commission scrutiny. The present Auditor General and his predecessor in that office have strenuously supported such a development. Although that question at first gave rise to considerable argument, the suggestion has now been incorporated in this bill. Also, the legislation establishes the Auditor General as an employer in his own right, so to speak. He will be able to establish classification levels for his own staff. As the Auditor General has indicated, he considered those particular matters as being of the utmost importance to him. Such provisions represent a major departure from the past, inasmuch as the Public Service Commission has had complete jurisdiction over the staff of the Auditor General and has treated it in the same way as it has treated the staff of other government departments.
The Auditor General, in conformity with his increasing independence, will be empowered to make special reports to this House. If he feels that there has been inadequate allotment of funds, he will be entitled to ask for more money: he can come to parliament and present a petition for additional funding. Also, he is to be exempt from the provisions of the Financial Administration Act which require appropriation requests to be divided into various categories, as is the case with respect to government departments. Basically, we are witnessing the creation of a piece of machinery, as it were, within the parliamentary structure which under the new act will be independent in its operation. Over the years this bill will make increasingly important the position of the Auditor General and will lead to attention being more sharply focused on the kinds of people who will fill that position from time to time.
What will be the scope of his work? Once this bill is passed, the Auditor General will be entitled to report on anything of significance which he feels should be brought to the attention of the House. He will, of course, retain his traditional duties. In addition, he will be entitled to say if the government has received value for money spent, if money has been spent without due regard for economy or efficiency, and point out instances where there are not, in his view, adequate procedures to measure and report on the effectiveness of programs. I am somewhat concerned about this provision and I am certain hon. members of the House will want to reflect on it, as well, when the bill is considered in committee.
The Auditor General has said that he looks on this bill as a landmark for the accounting profession of this country. I think many in the private sector will also be interested to see what kinds of powers the government, as a corporation, as it were, is granting its shareholders to audit, to use a term normally used in the private sector. Possibly we may receive representations from members of the public on this point. In certain respects

April 26, 1977
Auditor General Act
this bill represents a major departure from accepted practice within the accounting and auditing profession. Our Auditor General is to comment on matters which in the past have been considered as coming under the complete responsibility of internal management. For my part, I am somewhat concerned as to what is intended under this clause. I think that hon. members in committee had better consider it carefully before either subscribing to it fully or amending or changing it in any way.
The other point I wish to raise is the appointment of the comptroller general. I congratulate the President of the Treasury Board for having taken this step, which I know has been discussed at length in committee. I appreciate how significant such an appointment is for those who exercise political responsibility at the federal level, and also for those in senior civil service positions who must wonder how the new appointment will affect their own responsibilities. One can only say that major corporations in the private sector have encountered the same difficulties in the last 30 years and we are now seeing the government catch up to what has been accepted, normal practice in the industrial sphere for some time.
We simply cannot run a budget of some $44 billion annually without having an official in a senior financial position within the over-all structure responsible for dealing with questions of financial administration in each of the many departments and agencies and Crown corporations which make up that structure.
I also welcome the news that there is ultimately to be a new Crown corporation act placed before parliament. This is an area about which those of us who sit on the public accounts committee have had reason to be somewhat concerned in the last six months or so. I hope the comptroller general will have the authority to deal with senior officials of the corporations at the highest financial level. 1 understand that at the present time the financial branch of Treasury Board, which is endeavouring to fill the place which the comptroller will occupy, does not have that kind of link. This is an important consideration, bearing in mind the need to satisfy the Canadian public that money which has been voted for expenditure on various programs has indeed been handled in an appropriate and satisfactory manner.
The appointment of a comptroller general emanates from the recommendation made by the Auditor General in his 1976 report. He hinted at such a proposal a year earlier, in 1975, which indicates he must have given considerable thought to his final recommendation when he made it. I congratulate the President of the Treasury Board on the manner in which he has taken up this recommendation and discussed it with many interested groups including members of the public accounts committee and members of parliament generally, satisfying himself that this appointment is justified before setting about persuading those who might have needed persuasion to accept it as government policy.

Again in this context I would make reference to the public accounts committee. I believe this committee is an important one as, indeed, are all our committees. I feel, very often, that the work which members do in committee is overlooked in terms of attention from the media. People tend to think that if a member is not in his seat in this chamber, he cannot be very busy on parliament hill. I see a few members of the public accounts committee here this afternoon. I should like to think that some of the questioning of witnesses which went on in that committee over the last three years, and the conclusions drawn from those sittings, had some effect in encouraging both the President of the Treasury Board and his predecessor to move toward making the appointment provided for in the bill.
Members of the public accounts committee will, I know, feel a great deal more relaxed, when financial details provided by various departments and Crown agencies come before us, in the knowledge that before long a senior official in Treasury Board will be directing his attention to these areas in a thorough manner. I look forward to the speedy passage of the bill and a more detailed examination of its provisions in committee in the near future.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to follow the thoughtful speech of the vice-chairman of the public accounts committee.
I believe it is important that we should put the debate on this bill into perspective. You will recall, sir, that the former auditor general, Mr. Maxwell Henderson, seemed to take considerable delight in embarrassing the government, and I think the government was openly relieved when the time for his retirement came. His distinguished successor made it clear that he saw the auditor general as taking a quieter and less sensationalistic stance. At that point, 1 believe, the government was under the impression that the days of its public reoasting were over. That was before the new Auditor General saw the books. When he did open the books, he had certain things to say. It is in light of the statements he then made that we must deal with the bill before us. I should like to quote some of them. In his report on the public accounts for 1975, Mr. Macdonell said:
The present state of the financial management and control system of departments and agencies of the government of Canada is significantly below acceptable standards of quality and effectiveness.
I want to pause there and ask members of the House of Commons: how about that as a judgment upon an organization which had planned budgetary expenditures of $34 billion for the year ending March 31, 1976, and has increased its spending by at least 15 per cent in that year while asking everyone else to keep the lid on? That was not all the Auditor General had to say. Dealing with Crown corporations, he said this:
In the majority of the Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control is weak and ineffective. Moreover, co-ordination and guidance by control management agencies of financial management and control practices in the Crown corporations are virtually non-existent.
That is not merely a comment, Mr. Speaker; that is an indictment. Then comes the paragraph of the year against which we must set this bill. Mr. Macdonell, leading with the
April 26, 1977

statement that he was "driven inescapably" to this conclusion, said:
Based on the study of the systems of departments, agencies and Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control in the government of Canada is grossly inadequate. Furthermore, it is likely to remain so until the government takes strong, appropriate and effective measures to rectify this critically serious situation.
These points are more than an indictment; they are a condemnation by a man whose reputation in his profession both outside and within the public sector is beyond reproach,
In the report from which I quoted the Auditor General asked the government to consider the appointment of a comptroller general to attempt, perhaps for the first time, to lock the door before the horses had run away. What was the response of the government in 1976, during the course of the question period? They did not lock the door of the barn. They decided to repaint it. They wanted to appoint a royal commission to determine whether or not the results of the study which had been made by the Auditor General were justified and ought to be carried through. They argued that somehow or other they had to protect the sacred tradition of ministerial responsibility; that somehow or other the proposal made by the Auditor General was an attack on the concept of ministerial responsibility.
The President of the Treasury Board, who was being congratulated today for his sudden change of heart, at that time was arguing and defending the indefensible. Like a host of other members of parliament who care about our institutions but think some things are a little creaky and ancient and perhaps could be changed, I took a good look at the defence of ministerial responsibility which was raised and tried to find where the Auditor General had attacked that concept. I shall have something to say about that later in my speech. However, I wondered whether the defence raised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the President of the Treasury Board was really a valid one at all.
People outside the House of Commons who scrutinized the question, students of this institution and of other institutions, informed members of the parliamentary press gallery and observers of the parliamentary scene-not one of them defended the argument that was put up, namely that of ministerial responsibility. Not one of them took any issue at all with the comments of the Auditor General at that time and said it was an attack on the concept of ministerial responsibility.
The government persisted in its argument and appointed a royal commission. One of the members resigned in anger. The royal commission never got off the ground. The reason was that if royal commissions are to function, they have to examine some problem, question or some reasonable doubt which has arisen in the mind of the government. There was none such to look at. Finally, and gradually, the truth began to dawn on this government that perhaps the concept of ministerial responsibility was not being attacked at all and that the Auditor General was right.
Auditor General Act
The financial affairs of the people of this country are in a mess and something has to be done to put them on the road back. Yesterday, in the speech of the President of the Treasury Board, the government trumpeted the appointment of a comptroller general of Canada. There has been no one on the road to Damascus like the President of the Treasury Board. Some members have congratulated him, and I always like to congratulate those who have managed to seek redemption on the deathbed of the government. I always view confession as a good thing-somewhat cleansing, perhaps. The headlines in today's Ottawa Citizen say it all: "Government flip-flops to name spending overseer". This is exactly what has happened.
Speaking truthfully and strongly, I think the President of the Treasury Board knows very well that 1 share in the delight of many people that, at the end of this road along which the government are moving, they have at last seen the light and recognize that perhaps a comptroller general is a good thing. Quite frankly, I have some concern whether people who make these sudden conversions do it with their whole heart. All of us in the opposition-we might as well serve notice-the people of Canada and all the commentators who have been watching the situation will take a long, hard look at how the office of the comptroller general of Canada develops. Whether it is in fact a genuine conversion which will lead to genuine action, only the future can tell. I think even the President of the Treasury Board understands that we will be watching how the process develops.
1 understand that the new comptroller general of Canada will be responsible to the President of the Treasury Board. He will be appointed at the deputy minister level and will be responsible for the quality and integrity of the financial system, but not for policy. His office will absorb the present financial controls section of Treasury Board. There will be fundamental links with department heads, but decentralized control will be maintained. We shall have to see how that works out. At a guess, Mr. Speaker, this means there will not be departmental comptrollers as recommended by the Auditor General. The minister may differ and may want to clear that up in closing second reading debate, but in any event his statement was rather hazy on that point. Lastly, the comptroller general will be considered to be the government's chief financial administrator. In view of the words of the Auditqr General which I quoted earlier in my speech, I think this system is long overdue.
Might I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and at eight o'clock I will continue with some other matters that I want to raise in connection with ministerial responsibility which the President of the Treasury Board defended so mightily last year.

April 26, 1977
Solar Energy
