subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING DOMESTIC AND INDUSTRIAL USE OF SOLAR ENERGY
speechtext:
Motion No. 1.
That Bill C-309, an act respecting the domestic and industrial use of solar energy, be amended in clause 2 by striking out lines 20 to 27 at page 1 and substituting the following therefor:
"2. The Institute for Solar Energy Application (hereinafter the "Institute") is
hereby established as a corporation without share capital."
Motion No. 2.
That Bill C-309, an act respecting the domestic and industrial use of solar energy, be amended by inserting immediately after line 27 at page 1, the following new clause:

"3. (1) The affairs of the Institute shall be managed by a board of directors
composed of not fewer than ten and not more than 25 members of the
Institute who are Canadian citizens and who shall serve without remuneration.
(2) Directors shall be elected by the members of the Institute", and by renumbering the subsequent clauses accordingly.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the amended bill and the motions before us reflect for the most part advice received from hon. members on both sides of the House at the time this bill was discussed clause by clause in committee.
In particular, motion No. 2 proposes to increase from ten to 25 the number of members who can sit on the board of directors of the Institute of Solar Energy Application. Second, the motion proposes that these directors will be drawn from the membership of the Institute. We have, therefore, deleted the idea of appointing directors to the board of the institute, and replaced it with the idea of having all directors elected to the board.
In committee, and also on other occasions, the urgency of encouraging and promoting the creation of a Canadian industry producing solar energy technology and parts was stressed. This priority finds concise expression in clause 3(a) of the bill as reported to the House from committee.
Last Wednesday President Carter delivered his energy plan to the U.S. Congress. It is worth noting that President Carter calls for accelerating the use of solar energy where the use of renewable energy sources can replace the use of conventional fuels. This is good news. May I say if we wait too long in Canada to develop a viable solar technology suitable for production, Canada's manufacturers may not be able to compete even on the home market against technology produced abroad.	'
Let us look for a moment at what President Carter said last Wednesday. He said:
Our fourth strategy is to develop permanent and reliable new energy sources.
The most promising is solar energy, for which much of the technology is already available. Solar water heaters and space heaters are ready for commercialization. All they need is some incentive to initiate the growth of a large market.
Therefore, I am proposing a gradually decreasing tax credit, to run from now through 1984, for those who purchase approved solar heating equipment. Initially, it would be 40 per cent of the first $1,000 and 25 per cent of the next $6,400 invested.
Increased production of geothermal energy can be ensured by providing the same tax incentives as for gas and oil drilling operations.
In addition to the tax credit and the tax incentive just mentioned, President Carter proposed a business investment tax credit whereby the solar industry would be aided further by the inclusion of investments in solar equipment for industrial and commercial purposes among the approved conservation measures eligible for the proposed 10 per cent tax credit for energy saving investments. He went on to say:
The federal government will demonstrate its confidence in solar technology by undertaking a three-year solar program for federal buildings with up to $100 billion.
States are urged to amend their property tax laws to exempt solar installations from assessments, to enact legislation to protect access to the sun, and to
April 26, 1977

promote consumer education in the solar field. State public utility commissions would be required to develop guidelines to prevent utilities from discriminating against users of solar energy or other alternative energy sources.
A new office of small-scale technology is proposed within the department of energy in order to tap more fully the great potential of the nation's individual inventors and small business firms.
These are pretty vigorous measures on the part of our neighbour. I am putting them on record because our government will want, 1 am sure, to take a good look at these measures and propose soon a comprehensive Canadian package on renewable sources of energy rooted in the Canadian experience and the Canadian situation. Against this background of United States proposals, Bill C-309 almost disappears in significance. It does represent a small step in the right direction. It also offers a focus for parliamentary contributions here in the House of Commons, and hopefully soon in the Senate.
I wish to thank hon. members for their advice and support in committee, and I wish to say how impressed I was at the number of members who have spoken to me in support of the idea in the bill. In addition, I have received many letters of support, particularly from western Canada. I should like to ask for the support of the House at this report stage and on third reading today.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING DOMESTIC AND INDUSTRIAL USE OF SOLAR ENERGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to congratulate the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) on this excellent bill which he is presenting. We in the Conservative party certainly support research in solar energy. We are very concerned about finding alternate energy supplies. Bill C-309, which is an act respecting the domestic and industrial use of solar energy, is to be amended by striking out a number of clauses.
Earlier this year a news release from the minister's office in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources read:
The role of renewable energy in Canada's future received a boost from the federal government today.
Energy, Mirfes and Resources Minister Alastair Gillespie announced that:
-renewable energy has been awarded the largest share of a $10 million increase in federal energy R and D spending, for the fiscal year 1977-78;
-a renewable energy resource branch has been established within the energy policy sector of EMR; and
-a national advisory committee on conservation and renewable energy is being created.
My concern here is that it looks like we have some duplication. The government is proposing to establish a similar committee to that which the hon. member for Davenport is proposing. This duplication was discussed in committee in some detail.
The news release further read:
In the near future Canada and the rest of the world will have to begin to make greater use of renewable energy sources.
Conventional sources of energy will dominate our energy picture for some time, but renewable energy forms will play an increasing role in our energy supplies of the future.
In the committee proceedings on March 30 of this year the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Dupras) also commented on the fact that the
Solar Energy
minister had announced that there would be a national advisory committee on conservation and renewable energy. The parliamentary secretary went on to say:
That brings me to my first comment on this bill, Mr. Chairman. In so far as to the proposed Institute of Solar Energy Application will be a source of advice to the government and a visible demonstration of our commitment to exploiting renewable energy resources, those functions could well be duplicated .. .
y
We have a situation here where the government and the hon. member for Davenport are presenting duplicate proposals with regard to renewable energy and solar energy. The hon. member for Davenport pointed out that his bill goes further, that he wants to do a number of other things not contained in the government's proposal. I do not see why the government committee cannot incorporate the additional proposals presented in Bill C-309.
I pointed out another concern at the committee meetings. There is so much involvement in solar energy at this time that one wonders whether another body becoming involved in solar energy is really necessary. I will give an example of the number of organizations involved in solar energy research today. We have the Solar Energy Society of Canada. Manitoba has shown great leadership in this field. In Manitoba we have the University of Manitoba involved in research. The Biomass Energy Institute of Manitoba was formed many years ago and it has really shown leadership in research, in biomass, in solar energy. There is also the Morden Experimental Farm, plus commercial institutions such as the Canada Grains Council, the Canadian Wheat Board, and the Canadian Grain Commission. The parliamentary secretary mentioned that the government is going to establish its own advisory commission. Therefore there are certainly many bodies involved in research into solar energy.
We in the Conservative party have studied this in some detail. We will find out later this afternoon whether the government is going to talk out this bill. In any event we would like to make some alternate proposals which could be incorporated in Bill C-309 or in the government's advisory group.
The present government non-policy regarding solar energy will prove detrimental to Canada's future. An alternative policy, which encourages the use of solar and wind energy, will have at least three results: first, the life of Canada's limited fossil fuel reserves will be extended and the demand for costly new electrical capacity will be reduced. Second, development of solar heating systems and WECS will allow more money to be freed for more important, non-energy related, investment. Third, solar heating systems will create new investment opportunities for small businesses.
It seems desirable to adopt certain policies favourable to solar energy usage. It seems that little government money should be used for original research. Much of the research currently under way in the United States is directed at squeezing out the last morsel of efficiency from solar heating systems. The systems presently being developed are good enough. Also, it is doubtful as to whether Canadian research could ever

April 26, 1977
Solar Energy
catch up to the American level. Any Canadian research would probably overlap more intensive research being conducted in countries such as Japan or the United States.
There should be grants to encourage Canadian industry to develop solar energy equipment. The minimal research required to develop a basic solar heating and cooling system can easily be conducted in the private sector. However, they need encouragement. A certain proportion of the available money should be allocated for this use by small businesses.
There should be a guarantee by Central Mortgage and Housing of mortgages taken out for solar systems.
There should also be economic incentives for a limited time, for example, 1978 to 1984, to encourage homeowners to use available solar technology. This could be accomplished through a lump sum tax credit such as 25 per cent of the value of the solar system. A tax credit of 5 per cent of the value of a system for five years might act as a greater inducement, by bringing the amortized payments on a solar system down near the level of annual conventional fuel costs. Low interest mortgage rates may be another means of encouraging solar energy use. By the mid-1980's these economic incentives would not be necessary as the "cross-over" point for both oil and electricity will have been reached.
The United States has shown leadership. Recently a bill was presented to Congress. It states that solar energy as an important energy source may be many years away, but it is important that we get a start in this energy source now if solar energy is to become an important energy source in the future.
Under the U.S. bill, a credit against individual income tax liability is allowed for 40 per cent of the first $1,000 and 20 per cent of the second $1,000, for a maximum credit of $600, of the amount spent on installing qualified solar energy equipment on a principal residence owned by the individual paying for the installation.
The United States has also shown leadership in the implementation of solar energy. There is an excellent magazine entitled "Solar Engineering". It points out that in southern California the Edison Company is going to operate its first ten megawatt solar plant. In addition, energy research and development funds are being provided for heating and cooling large shopping centres in the United States.
We should adopt many of the proposals and much of the research conducted in the United States. If we did that, it would not be long until Canada was on a par with the United States with regard to the promotion of and research into solar energy.
Regardless of whether the government lets this bill pass or talks it out and proposes its own committee, we certainly fully support information on, research into, and development of solar energy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a few words to indicate our support for this bill. I believe it is time for Canada to leave aside all efforts made in the past

regarding non renewable energy sources. As we can see it from year to year, this kind of energy will not last forever. Therefore, we must absolutely turn towards renewable energy sources and if we have a few million dollars to invest, I believe it is time for Canada to follow the example of the United States, which have succeeded in outpacing us in this regard. As a matter of fact, the Liberal spokesman indicated earlier how the United States have encouraged efforts made by both the government and companies willing to invest in solar energy development and in research in this field.
I think that so far we have directed our efforts toward nuclear energy and have not given enough thought to solar energy, because we know perfectly well that the latter does not carry the same disadvantages as nuclear energy. It has not yet been demonstrated that such disadvantages could be overcome, and that is why I must congratulate the mover of the bill before us. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that we shall not confine ourselves to the report stage today and shall let this bill go through the House, because we are already late and it is time to turn once and for all towards solar energy. In my opinion and in that of the majority of Canadians, this energy is the least hazardous and safest of all energy sources. It is merely a matter for the government to give adequate incentives to those who will produce the necessary equipment, to those who will carry out research in this field so that we can develop as much as possible this new process called solar energy. I believe Canada should once more follow the lead of the United States-and for once, it is a good example to follow-and I am convinced that all hon. members of this House cannot but agree to such a bill. We hope it will be passed today.

Mr. Speaker, I am certainly not going to retard the passage of this commendable initiative by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). There is a certain touch of irony, quite frankly, in that, given the nature of our concern with all forms of energy, when you compare the relevant performance of this government with that of the United States administration, both past and present. In the alternate energy field, there is no comparison whatsoever.
I was, quite frankly, flabbergasted by the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last week to the effect that President Carter had obviously taken some of his energy policy from Canada. Nothing could be farther from the truth when one looks at the performance of this government, and nowhere is it more so than in the energy field. I have already put on the record in previous speeches the comparison-the minister knows what it is-in percentage and per capita terms, between this government and that of the U.S.
There is more than a touch of irony that it would be the initiative of a back bench member which would focus on the need for some kind of effective research into and promotion of solar energy. In fact I heard as recently as today that we have in Canada exactly the same number of nuclear plants as solar
April 26, 1977

heated homes. That gives you some idea of the extent of commitment which currently exists at the federal level with respect to the use of development of solar energy. One can only hope that this initiative of the hon. member for Davenport will be an additional prod to the government to take seriously the development of alternate energy.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) has suggested, a tremendous amount of research has been done in the U.S. in this area and we hope we will be able to make good use of it. One would have to recognize the fact that there will have to be some additional research, because obviously in a sophisticated area of solar energy, and given the particular situation of Canada with its more northern climate, we will have to develop an approach which would be more appropriate to our own situation. The initiative of the hon. member may help us at least to become conscious of that. While I realize there is a prohibition of any financial commitment in a private member's bill, one hopes that the sheer initiative in the House agreeing to this proposal might wake up the government to take seriously its responsibilities in this area. It has only recently become aware that it even has a responsibility in this area. If the focus of this bill can be an additional spur for the government to take action in the field of solar energy, so much the better.
I feel this to be particularly important because I come from a province which relies heavily on offshore petroleum, which is very expensive and which makes it very difficult for us to put the province of P.E.I. and indeed the whole of the Atlantic region, into the mainstream of the national economy. Therefore I will not say anything further at this time. I hope that in this measure we can have greater and more serious attention from the government to solar energy and other forms of renewable energy.

Mr. Speaker, I have been reluctant to rise to my feet because I did not want to run the risk of contributing to the talking out process which we experience so often during this hour. However, since it appears that that process is set aside for today and that this bill will get through, I should like to indicate that we give it our full support.
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), with a modesty that we do not often witness on that side of the House, said that this was a very small bill and that in time it might fade into insignificance when grander things are done. I can only say to him that the first step is the all important one, and he is to be congratulated on the initiative he has taken. I am not concerned, and I do not think the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) is either, about the number of bodies and agencies interested in solar energy. It is a new area and it takes a number of bodies really interested to set something moving, and certainly it takes quite a bit to get the present government moving. I hope that is what is happening by our passing this bill this afternoon, as I trust we shall do. Again I extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Davenport.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before discussing those matters which I said prior to the supper hour I would discuss, let me say to the minister, with regard to Bill C-20 respecting the Auditor General, that we share some concern about the wording used in clause 5 of the bill. We believe, frankly, that the standard accountancy words, "in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles" should be used instead of the words, "stated accounting policies of the federal government." I say this because the Auditor General himself cast doubt on the accounting policies of the federal government.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: But he himself endorsed this bill.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
We want to make sure that the bill gives the Auditor General a great deal of latitude to criticize. I am thinking especially of the wording of clause 7(2)(f>). I gather that the avoidance of the words which would normally be used in these circumstances is likely to restrict the Auditor General. That may not be the intention, but there is that possibility.
Further, clauses 5 and 7 do not use, as did Part VII of the Financial Administration Act, the words "consolidated revenue fund". This means that the Auditor General is not exclusively responsible for funds coming under the consolidated revenue fund. To carry out his responsibilities he could hire consultants, other auditing firms, to perform functions which formerly came under his exclusive responsibility. There is a danger that such firms will be less assiduous in the uncovering of information, and this bill creates some potential for patronage or favouritism. I hope this legislation will not be administered in the same way as the census matter was administered. We dealt with that matter recently.
We feel that Crown corporations should be exclusively under the Auditor General and that their audits should not be contracted out. I suggest that recent disputes which arose in the Public Accounts Committee demonstrate the validity of what I am saying. In the experience of that committee, private firms are reluctant or not likely to give the committee full information.
It is incongruous to me that there is not in this bill, as there was not in the old act, any need for the Auditor General to be a qualified accountant. Moreover, clause 5 does not refer to the Auditor General's "certifying the accounts." It refers to his expressing his opinion on their suitability. I suggest that a

requirement to prove an unwise expenditure places too heavy an onus on the Auditor General. Perhaps we should consider changing the requisite words in the bill to "value for money". Let him show if the government has obtained value for money. Perhaps we could accept some such concept.
As the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) suggested, all annual reports of all Crown corporations should automatically be referred to the relevant committees, which would deal with them.
As I said earlier, I am concerned about the entire question of government accountability. If we are at all concerned about these matters we ought to direct our minds to examining critically some of the theoretical, basic underpinnings of our form of government. In that regard it seems to me that the principle which has been twisted and stretched beyond reason, indeed beyond serviceability, is that of ministerial responsibility-
The doctrine of ministerial responsibility has two important facets. First, it presents a working assumption which is palpably untrue-that the minister is the source of policy decisions which he may have only rubber-stamped or of which perhaps he never heard. From this comes the second proposition-that if the House of Commons wishes to discuss factual or policy matters it must address itself to the public servants through the minister, and in maintaining the fiction that the minister is indeed responsible, the House is obliged to accept an intolerable amount of interference, real and implied, from him. To preserve this outdated nonsense is to view the workings and conflicts of government through a very dark glass.
The minister is at once the mouthpiece for the bureaucracy when it speaks to the Commons, and for the Commons when it speaks to the bureaucracy. Since the minister identifies more readily with the executive than with parliament, the latter is the loser in this conflict of interest. Parliament can call the public servants before its committees, but always with the knowledge that these witnesses must impose censorship on themselves or have it done for them. The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) made it clear in a previous portfolio that he controlled the appearances of his departmental officials before committees. It is obvious that committees cannot scrutinize the executive if their ability to do so is dependent on executive generosity.
The pre-eminence of the doctrine of ministerial responsibility blows away all the froth about parliamentary sovereignty, grievance before supply, and security of the executive, and leaves us with the totalitarian reality which is the Canadian House of Commons. All the constitutional formulations which were cited in the past to advance parliament's claims have been either abandoned or perverted to buttress executive authority. The cabinet is no longer, in the words of Walter Bagehot "a hyphen which joins, a buckle which fastens, the legislative part of the Senate to the executive part of the State." It is a fog that obscures, a wall that blocks. If we do not devise fundamental rule changes in the House of Com-
April 26, 1977

mons which explicitly challenge some of the more outlandish perversions of the idea of ministerial responsibility, then parliament will never again truly represent Canadians.
The starting point is in the House of Commons committees. We must take the risk of bringing a more public dimension to the advice of public servants. In fact this is already done in most of the public media, and this realism in recognizing that public servants hold, and consistently advance, certain ideas should be accepted in committees. Our committees should have the power to call any public servant to testify, under oath if required, backed up by subpoena powers. To concentrate discussion, committees should have access to more than the procedural advice they now are primarily restricted to, and have adequate staff resources under the control of the House of Commons. We should extend the practice of committees being chaired by opposition members, perhaps in proportion to party strength in the House. Committees should be encouraged to prepare thorough reports which will merit serious attention from the House, the press, and the civil service.
Keeping in mind that ultimately the House and the committees are still controlled by the government's majority, I do not see why senior appointments should be the exclusive preserve of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). At present the Commissioner of Official Languages is appointed pursuant to a resolution of the House. Why not deputy ministers, the Chairman of the National Capital Commission, the Clerk of the Privy Council-all after appropriate hearings by the relevant standing committee? A parliamentary committee backed up by proper staff could, through a confirmation hearing, do more to bring senior public servants down to ground level than any number of 90-minute evasive committee meetings on estimates.
There are complementary rule changes which must be pursued. We should end the automatic supply guillotine provision for five of six departments per year; these estimates would receive approval when the House was satisfied with explanations received from ministers. The estimates themselves should be presented in greater detail, with more specific vote headings, in place of the omnibus categories which presently lump together millions of dollars in diverse expenditures. Our private members' hour is widely recognized as farcical and changes shuuld be made to bring more measures to a vote. The Ontario legislature has recently done this with positive results. We in the Progressive Conservative Party will continue to insist that the "just society" and "open government" once trumpeted so loudly by the Prime Minister are empty platitudes without a forthright freedom of information bill. Let us have an end to the degrading spectacle of Canadians flying to Washington to obtain information about their own government.
I do not believe Canadians can afford to let the House of Commons remain where it is now. Either we must return to the era when the House of Commons had real power through a widespread ability to delay all types of government business, or we must move to terminate the omnipotence of the dogma of
Auditor General Act
ministerial responsibility. One way or the other, genuine scrutiny must be the purpose of the House of Commons.
We are unlikely to see this. We shall probably see an extension of the process begun in 1969, routinely to cut off legislative debate at the instance of the government. This will complete the degradation of parliament, ending its coercive powers. Members of parliament will be left with trivial tasks at the expense of fulfilling their constitutional role. And better government will not be the result.
The greatest loss to parliament over the last century has been the impossibility of a "sense of the House"-the crossparty acceptance of what is clearly right and rejection of what is clearly wrong. Instead, the House has subdivided itself into rigid parties and factions which carry rhetoric far past the point needed to give the public a clear and meaningful choice. We have acted as if "ministerial responsibility" were the only constitutional principle worth guarding, and as a result have eviscerated parliament's mandate to scrutinize the executive. Perhaps T.V. will compel a change in behaviour. We can hope, but I think it is time for parliament and the public to ask fundamental questions.
The present session is considered by many observers to be the least productive in many years. A strange political encephalitis seems to have infected the House of Commons, and the political focus of attention has shifted to the press conferences, to the radio and T.V. interview rooms and the federal-provincial conferences. The government House leader seems to believe that the desultory debate on the government's desultory legislative program is evidence of a disinclination on the part of the opposition to pass anything. As opposition House leader, I believe both he and the Prime Minister must be pleased with the approaching successful conclusion of the campaign begun in 1968 to denude the House of Commons totally of constitutional significance.
Public interest in the proceedings of the House of Commons seems to be confined to the daily question period. For all its drama, excitement, and occasional comedy, the question period is not well suited to enforcing the responsibility of the executive to the House of Commons, and does so only at the most superficial level. Any attempt to advance policies or put interpretation on matters in the question period is expressly forbidden by our rules. As it has evolved, our question period provides a forum for commentary on urgent matters arising on a day to day basis outside the House. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, few of the members of the press gallery who crowd in for the question period stay for the debates. This point was made abundantly clear by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) yesterday. It is not really surprising because the legislative debates in the House are prolonged and are frequently beside the point at issue. I think my hon. friend will admit that. Since both the government House leader and I accept this fact, it may be legitimately wondered why nothing is done to change things.

April 26, 1977
Auditor General Act
If the legislative process could be viewed in isolation, there would be no great difficulty in making changes. However, when it is realized that legislative debate represents for the individual member of a party the sole remaining opportunity to make a stand and compel the attention of the executive, the dilemma becomes clearer. Two or more days may be adequate to debate and decide on the merits of a particular bill, but it is not long enough if such a debate represents the only significant opportunity to debate Wheat Board policy, environmental policy, or northern development. We do not have this opportunity in the Chamber today.
Nor is it long enough for the opposition to bring forcefully to a minister's attention the objections of affected constituents. It may take five, ten or 15 days to bring a minister seriously to consider objections he would at first prefer to ignore. When concessions are obtained the debate ends. In the meantime, debate is tedious and repetitious. The process dignifies no one and pleases no one. Prolonged debate is a blunt weapon, but unfortunately in the modern Canadian House of Commons the only one.
I enjoy this place, Mr. Speaker, and the camaraderie here, but I think it must be evident to anyone who sits in this House from time to time that we are really out of touch with some realities. We do not have the opportunity to debate the great issues of the day. Our procedures should be examined, not just in terms of shortness of time but in terms of upgrading them so that members of parliament have the opportunity to represent their constituents in a way that their constituents believe they should be represented.
I have suggested that we must, in addition to examining a bill like this, also examine the basic principles which are the underpinning of our parliamentary democracy, that we must indeed examine the machinery of parliamentary democracy itself. I think it is important to this place that that be done, and I hope that this bill will provide the opportunity to begin the real debate on that issue.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members know that this is not the first time that a bill having to do with the Auditor General is before the House. I suspect the last time was November, 1970. However, that bill was withdrawn after much protest, primarily because it was discovered that it would muzzle the Auditor General.
Presently the Auditor General operates under the provisions of the Financial Administration Act which devotes some 10 sections to the appointment of and instructions to the Auditor General. The proposal before the House has been praised and supported by the Auditor General himself. It appears that members of committees who have studied the office of the Auditor General have had most of their suggestions accepted in this bill. Even though we on this side of the House have agreed with many of the provisions of the bill, I do not think we would be doing our job if we did not point out that there are still some shortcomings.
Notably, Mr. Speaker, the bill fails to address itself to the Crown corporation situation. Specifically, the government still

has not put legislation before us in any way to define a Crown corporation or even to determine the number of Crown corporations or agencies. To take this a step further, we are still not clear from the proposal of the government who should be doing the audits of these Crown corporations and agencies.
The powers of the Auditor General and of the Public Accounts Committee is another area which has not been adequately put before the House. The report of the Independent Review Committee on the Office of the Auditor General had this to say about his powers, in paragraph 17 of chapter 6:
The Auditor General should have the right of access to financial records and documents of all Crown corporations of which he is not the auditor, as he deems necessary to the fulfilment of his responsibilities as auditor of the accounts of Canada.
It became obvious recently in the Public Accounts Committee that neither the committee itself nor the Auditor General had power to obtain information or even to call witnesses who might be deemed necessary. For example, I refer to the Polysar issue in regard to which the Public Accounts Committee was denied information which was desired in order to consider its decision and to make its ultimate report to this House as directed by the House.
Furthermore, although the Auditor General sat in on all of the committee hearings and deliberations in connection with Polysar, he was not able to participate in any way; he was there simply as an observer at the invitation of our committee. This was because the Auditor General, who had been the co-auditor of that Crown corporation, was "fired", which is the word that is being used. What actually happened, of course, was that the shareholders-the shareholders being the Government of Canada-at their annual meeting failed to re-appoint the Auditor General, so that in effect he lost his appointment. Anyway he was no longer co-auditor of Polysar, and Polysar no longer came under his jurisdiction.
It was only because the House of Commons, under special reference, gave the reference to the Public Accounts Committee that Polysar was under examination by that committee. However, if servants of this House are not to have the power to obtain the information they need, the House will suffer, and therefore the people of Canada will suffer.
During those hearing things were so indefinite in the existing regulations that the committee was unable to determine whether Polysar was a Crown corporation. If it was not, if was unable to determine what date it ceased to be a Crown corporation. The brief history is that Polysar, which had been entirely owned by the Government of Canada, and was therefore a Crown corporation, was sold. The shares were sold by the Government of Canada to the Canada Development Corporation which at that time was wholly owned by the Government of Canada. However, because it was a corporation of its own, it was argued that Polysar was owned by CDC and was no longer a Crown corporation. At some time later in 1975 a portion of the shares of CDC was sold to the public. Therefore the government ceased to be the sole owner through CDC of Polysar.
April 26, 1977

The Financial Administration Act contains a Schedule D which, as of this day, still lists the Polymer Corporation, the predecessor of Polysar, as being a Crown corporation. The government tells us there will be something done in the near future to remove that name as a Crown corporation. We have conflicting evidence as to whether the Crown corporation is or is not a Crown corporation. We would like to see clarification on issues such as that.
During those hearings the Public Accounts Committee was given certain letters and was given certain evidence which contained blanks. It was very difficult to tell whether the information that was being kept from the committee was necessary because it was not there. One can hardly make a judgment without the adequate information.
We have had revelations today, inside the House and outside the House, referring to possible grave consequences to the Government of Canada because of references to Dutch customers who have been discovered by an agency outside the control of the House of Commons.
