subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not proposing to debate proceedings in committee. I was merely using that to lay the groundwork for the argument I was planning to use tonight.
I would like to move now to the remarks of the minister himself. The minister has indicated that it is the government's intention to present draft Crown corporation legislation for consideration by the House in the very near future. He indicated that the legislation had resulted from extensive and detailed study of the complexities involved in the government's desire to clarify and strengthen the direction and control of Crown corporations. Mr. Speaker, I hope you will see that this ties in with my reference earlier, and that was the purpose of that reference. I am hopeful that it will contain a definition of what is and what is not a Crown corporation. I hope it will then be possible for the government, or somebody within the government, to have the responsibility and the ability to pin down the number of Crown corporations and agencies that exist.
There is a further very important aspect of this, that is, the audit of these Crown corporations and agencies. 1 may refer a little later to the audit of these corporations, but I would like to refer now to the report of the Independent Review Commit-
Auditor General Act
tee on the Office of the Auditor General of Canada. In chapter 6, recommendation No. 15, they concluded the following:
The Auditor General should audit the financial accounts of all Crown corporations whose expenditures directly affect the budgetary accounts of Canada.
In recommendation No. 16 they said the following:
The audit of commercially oriented and financially self-sufficient Crown corporations should be conducted either by the Auditor General or by accounting firms, as deemed appropriate in each case.
That argument may rage for a while yet until it is determined who should be the auditor of Crown corporations and just where the Auditor General's responsibilities should end. The instructions under the Financial Administration Act are not clear. I submit that the instructions under the bill before us are not clear as far as Crown corporations are concerned.
I am also hoping that the government is not asking us to pass a framework kind of a bill once again. That is where we would have a bill that is bare bones and that has a lot of regulations coming later on which parliament does not get a chance to express an opinion. There are people who have expressed opinions on where the Auditor General's responsibilities should begin and should end. It has been suggested by the former Auditor General that the accounts of all corporations, Crown and otherwise which are financed by public funds, should without exception be examined by and reported on to parliament by the Auditor General and no one else. He is not alone in this. I can see the desirability of such an action as that. On the other hand the present Auditor General himself has expressed some reservations on that because if he were called upon to perform all of the work that is performed on all corporations and agencies, Crown or where the Crown has any investment at all, he would soon have the biggest office in the country.
There are many corporations such as the Canada Development Corporation in which the government has a very large investment and the Auditor General is not the auditor. The government is the sole equity holder in Canadian National Railways and Air Canada. In those cases the Auditor General does not perform the audit.
I am not certain that it could be exclusively argued that Crown corporations which are in the commercial field should not be audited by private Firms of auditors. There has been the suggestion that patronage is handed out. I suppose everyone is entitled to have his business done by his friends. Whether that is patronage or calling upon a professionally qualified person, I am not certain.
Looking at the bill for a moment, I see that the provisions of it in some way duplicate the provisions of the Financial Administration Act as they are at the moment. Under clause 4 of the bill the Auditor General is considered to be a very important person indeed. There it is specified, as it was previously, that the Auditor General shall be paid a salary equal to the salary of the Chief Justice of the Federal Court of Canada.

that stronger action should be taken by auditors in cases when they find practices in the operations of their clients that are not, in their opinion, proper. However, it became apparent in the questioning that it is not easy to determine just where the responsibility of the auditor begins and ends.
A situation could develop where the auditor is expected to adopt the role of an ombudsman or even of a minister of consumer affairs, and the auditor might be put in the position of having to report on shortages of soup tins, on faulty procedures in the production of rusty Fords, or something like that, and 1 believe the thinking members of the profession would argue that the auditor's responsibility must end short of that. Perhaps in the Polysar example the auditor's responsibility was fulfilled when he reported to the audit committee of the board of directors on the practices that were of great concern to the auditing company.
The auditor has very few choices when it comes to the signing or not signing of his report. If he wishes to feel that he is the conscience of the company, he can report to the audit committee or to the board, but it is a much more serious thing when he wishes to qualify his statement, that is, to issue an unclear certificate on the statements on which he is reporting. In the case of Polysar those actions were taken and the practice continued until 1976. The Auditor General at that time satisfied himself apparently that he could sign a clear certificate. As we now know, he took further action which he felt was important, that is, to write to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
I think I should comment, before I conclude, on the announcement by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) of the creation of the position known as chief financial officer or comptroller general of Canada. We know that the Auditor General has been asking for such a position to be established for some three years. The minister has explained today there was a problem with terminology, and I can quite understand that one who has not spent a long time with accountancy books might misunderstand that. I certainly share the Auditor General's delight at having this position filled and knowing there will be someone who has the responsibility of reporting directly to the minister on expenditures of the government.
The minister himself referred to the size of the government and the need for improvements over and above the systems that were in effect some 20 years ago. I hope that he will provide guidance to managers in the departments, and that the departments will therefore be able to produce the useful information which will eventually prove useful to members of the House.
Late last year 1 had the honour to address a group of financial managers of the government, members of a strange group which is called the Financial Management Institute of the Institute of Financial Management. It is a kind of inside-out group, by the sound of it. One of the complaints of one of the financial managers was that the group cannot produce Cadillac reports with Model T equipment. I think that was an indication of the frustration felt by the financial managers in
Auditor General Act
the government who are trying to be effective civil servants and produce information that is wanted by the administration and by the House of Commons.
I am sorry that the minister seemed to waffle a little bit in his remarks when he made reference to the Glassco Commission. He referred to refining and improving what the Glassco Commission considered as essential safeguards for administrative integrity as if it might have been recent. It seems to me that the Glassco Commission report was a 1962 document and much has happened since then. It was obvious that a new system was necessary but, in the words of the Glassco report, such a system was beyond its terms of reference. It found lots of faults and suggested what should be done, but it was not within the commission's reference to design a system.
I certainly hope that the three new measures, this bill, the one that has been proposed, and the post of chief financial officer or comptroller general, will work together to achieve what the accountants of Canada and the Auditor General have been urging the government to do for three years.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
1 welcome this opportunity to speak in the debate on Bill C-20. This bill appoints a Comptroller General for Canada. That was announced by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) yesterday. He announced that the intention of the government is to create a position of comptroller general, its occupant to be the chief Financial administrator of the federal public service.
The minister also told hon. members that the proposed legislation respecting the office of the Auditor General is one of the more significant initiatives taken by the government to ensure that public funds are handled efficiently and effectively. Well, it is almost too little and too late. The government is appointing this Comptroller General literally dragged and screaming. It is not something it really wanted to do. It was forced into it because it has been completely exposed by the opposition and the present Auditor General. There has been complete and total mismanagement of the nation's business, with no proper accounting system whatsoever in any government department or Crown corporation.
It is interesting to note that the President of the Treasury Board stated:
I must say that I am heartened by the generally favourable nature of the Auditor General's comments on the adequacy of the measures taken to date.
It was most interesting to note that the Auditor General was in the public gallery this afternoon, which indicates that he has taken a genuine interest in this appointment.
I would like to give credit to the former leader of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), who through the last three federal elections called for the expansion of the Auditor General's office and for the government to be fully accountable. The proposal put forward now is merely something the Conservative party called for many years ago.

April 26, 1977
Auditor General Act
Two great revolts in the English speaking world were the parliamentary rebellion against Charles I, and the American Revolution. Each had its origin in the improper taking and spending of tax money of the people. Now, hundreds of years later, we find that we have gained nothing. In fact we have lost much ground because of the monstrous increase in spending, the complexity of government, and the inability of government and the people to be kept advised and aware of how much and the manner of government spending.
Starting in 1966, and each year through to 1972, the year of the last report of Mr. Maxwell Henderson, the former auditor general, he made clear comments about the weakening of parliamentary control of expenditure. This was not just through a philosophical statement; it was borne out and corroborated each year by a number of very carefully detailed illustrations. However, nothing was done, although something should have been done many years ago. I cannot give the government any credit for taking action at this late date. This action should have been taken many years ago.
To show that the foregoing was not just one man's opinion, the present Auditor General, Mr. Macdonell, said in his last report for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1976, at page 9:
I am deeply concerned that parliament and, indeed, the government has lost, or is close to losing, effective control of the public purse.
He expressed that concern a year earlier in his annual report, stating that the state of financial management and control systems of departments and agencies of the Government of Canada were significantly below the acceptable standards of quality and effectiveness. This is not just something which has cropped up in the last couple of months. It is something which has been in effect for many years under Liberal regimes.
Here is the best evidence possible that not only have the people through their parliament been unable to deal with official spending, but the government itself is largely clueless. And, with this, federal public spending estimates jumped from 1971-72 to 1977-78 from $14 billion to $41 billion, and during this time the government has been engaged in an attempt to kid us all by telling us solemnly that it is engaged in policies of restraint. What a joke. The Auditor General's response to the present government's accounting system was; and I quote:
We feel very strongly about the fact that unless the systems are corrected the day may well come when I cannot give a clear certificate on the accounts of Canada.
I contend that this gives a clear indication of the financial fiasco into which the Liberal government is leading Canada.
The financial implications of this are such that one must seriously wonder aloud why the government is employing accounting procedures which it would not accept were they used by a business or private citizen. Revenue officials have little patience for an individual whose books are not clear and accurate, yet the government is using methods about which the Auditor General has serious reservations.
The Liberal government has become a spending machine without a control centre. One need only look at some examples of financial mismanagement found in the Auditor General's

report. The Department of National Defence, at a time of a national housing crisis, lost $214,000 on unoccupied housing in Halifax where there was a severe housing shortage. The Department of Supply and Services wasted $3.8 million on a computerized government payroll system that was unworkable and had to be abandoned. The federal government paid $4.5 million for offices it did not use. The federal government has a bizarre practice of making loans to itself and counting the loans as assets.
The Auditor General's report, of course, is full of stories of federal government waste and mismanagement. Federal government spending has been growing at such a rapid rate that spending has gone from $7 billion to over $42 billion since 1962, and the civil service has nearly quadrupled, from 132,000 to about 458,000.
The stories go on and on. The waste and mismanagement of Canadian tax dollars are just incredible. In 1975 and again in 1976 the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation failed to record accrued interest amounting to $14 million on loans from Canada. The government agreed to pay an annual rent of $241,000 for a property that the previous tenant had been leasing at $48,000 a year. The Post Office Department failed to recover costs of trans-border services between Canada and the United States amounting to $55,000 to March 31, 1976.
In 1975 the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce intended to sell its interest in Radio Engineering Products Limited as soon as the company had become sufficiently stable to attract a buyer. This did not happen, and the company filed a declaration of bankruptcy. It was indebted to the government to the extent of $6 million. No significant recovery of the loss is expected. That is the history of this government for years and years. It is just unbelievable.
This country has seen massive balance of payments deficits. The latest current deficit was $1,363 billion in the last quarter of 1976, the worst in Canada's history. The new comptroller general is going to have his work cut out for him. He will probably go out of his mind after the first year trying to figure it all out. Canada is now running the largest foreign debt in the western world. What on earth is being done with all this money? What is happening on the benches opposite?
In the last ten years the budget has skyrocketed over 400 per cent, from $8.8 billion to a forecast $46 billion in this fiscal year. Total government spending per person was $2,900 per person in 1975. Government took in only $2,700 per person. Thus, government has proceeded to spend an additional inflationary $200 on each of us. Where is it all going?
Transfer payments of $21.4 billion represent a little more than half the current budget. Of these, more than $9 billion went directly to Canadian citizens in social welfare expenditures, such as old age security, family allowances and unemployment payments.
The national debt of the federal government will be around $28 billion at the end of the fiscal year, the result of budget deficits in 20 of the last 23 years. The interest on the national debt, which was already $1.2 billion in 1967, will be around
April 26, 1977

$4.6 billion at the end of this fiscal year, making it the third largest federal expenditure after health and welfare and economic development and support.
The government has also contracted to guarantee the borrowings of Crown corporations such as Air Canada and the CBC. Last year the government guaranteed $15.5 billion in loans and advances to Crown corporations. Federal spending has grown faster in the past ten years than the private economy which supports it. During the last fiscal year expenditures for the Liberal government's bilingual program reached $121 million. Federal employees, excluding the armed forces, were paid approximately $5 billion in 1975, about triple the $1.7 billion they were earning in 1965. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, there is no end to this mad spending. I do not think that the comptroller general will cure overnight this Liberal madness.
The problems the government is causing across the country are unbelievable. Today I received a letter from a shoe manufacturer operating in Ontario. He said:
I am talcing the liberty of enclosing a copy of an editorial ad of ours that appeared in the March 1977 issue of the Shoe and Leather Journal of Canada.
It is the first in a series of ads of similar theme which I intend to publish over the next 12 months.
In my opinion, the voice of the businessman is being heard less and less frequently in this country, particularly within earshot of Ottawa.
Accordingly, I have been forced to seek my own arena to express these ideas and opinions that are troubling our company, and for that matter, all businessmen in this country.
I hope you will find our editorial stimulating reading.
It is signed by Anthony J. Carrier, of the J. D. Carrier Shoe Co. Limited.
I have before me a copy of an advertisement put out by the Shoe and Leather Journal of March, 1977. The headline is, "Frankly we are troubled!" After listing a number of ways in which the government is affecting this business, and I might say that the points raised apply to other businesses right across this country, for everywhere one hears the same story of government interference, of rules and regulations strangling the growth of business, the advertisement goes on to say:
We are troubled by a government that mismanages public funds to the point that the Auditor General calls for an inquiry to check 'out of control' government spending.
The advertisement goes on to list a number of ways in which government involvement is affecting business in Canada.
Next I wish to refer to a news release put out by Treasury Board on February 16, 1977. The heading of the news release reads, "Public Service Growth Cut by Half-Authorized Man-Years to Increase by Six-Tenths of One Per Cent." The fourth paragraph of the news release reads in part:
The drastic cut-back in the growth of the Public Service reflects a comprehensive examination of departmental man-power requirements conducted by the Treasury Board secretariat, in consultation with departmental managers. It proved possible to cut, in absolute terms, the manpower resources allocated to some departments and agencies, so as to authorize higher-than-average increases in others to meet pressing demands.
Auditor General Act
In this news release the department tries to make out that the government is cutting back on the growth of the civil service. But I suggest this is not happening. The government is now expanding every federal department by hiring employees from private employment agencies.
I placed a series of questions on the Order Paper to discover how many people the government is hiring through private employment agencies. So far I have received figures relating to 16 departments. I have placed questions on the Order Paper relating to approximately another 20 departments. Following the recent revelation that we have in the order of 1,000 Crown corporations and federal government agencies in Canada, I can see that I shall need to place a tremendous number of questions on the Order Paper in order to determine how many people the government and Crown agencies are hiring through private employment agencies.
I have learned that 16 government departments hired 4,464 new people at a cost of between $7 million and $8 million. Yet, despite such hirings, the President of the Treasury Board has the gall to say that the government is cutting back on the growth of the civil service. It just shows you how dishonest the government is, and the sneaky methods it uses to expand the federal civil service.
I now wish to quote an article entitled "The Big Sleep", by Jacques Grenier. Underneath the title of the article appear the words, "There are now more than 300,000 federal civil servants, some of whom are awake." The author says this, among other things, in the article:
Because of the sheer size of the bureaucracy, a civil servant who wants to can go almost completely underground, performing little or no work.
On the one hand some civil servants are doing little or no work, and on the other the government is hiring employees through private employment agencies to staff government departments. Surely the comptroller general, after he is appointed, ought to investigate the undercover work mentioned in this article. I continue to quote:
A federal employee at the National Museums of Canada admitted to me he works about an hour a week. He makes over 515,000 a year. A bright young bureaucrat with the Foreign Investment Review Agency admits working about two hours a week. His salary is $28,000.
I certainly hope the comptroller general will look into the matters I have raised this evening. The article goes on to say:
An acquaintance of mine who has been in the civil service for four years, with a salary in excess of $20,000, confided. 'I took this job because I wanted to make some kind of difference. Now I'm working a total of about three hours a week. It's at something I don't like, and there is no real way out of it.' He is completely disillusioned.
Isn't that too bad! The article goes on to say:
From my own brief stint as a civil service information officer in Industry, Trade and Commerce, I can sympathize ...
Obviously, these employees do not have enough work. The article goes on to say:
... and when there are tasks, they seem meaningless. I discovered that working too fast simply left that much more time with nothing to do. Like the cubicles in the high-rise buildings, the bureaucratic workload is compartmentalized. Once you've finished the assigned work, there is usually little else to do. If you strike out on your own, you run the risk of trampling on someone else's jurisdiction.

April 26, 1977
Auditor General Act
There is built-in discouragement for someone trying to make work by finding other jobs to do to fill in his time.
The government is hiring thousands of employees through private employment agencies, and then has the gall to say it is cutting back on growth in the civil service. How deceitful can you be?
A number of hon. members this evening have commented on the accountability of Crown corporations. Mr. Speaker, Crown corporations and government agencies in Canada are accountable to no one. At present they can do what they want, and the amount of covering up done is unbelievable. Let me use what happens in Air Canada as an example.
I suggest that the new comptroller genera! should place an examination of Air Canada accounting procedures high on his list of priorities. Let me cite some examples of what I mean. In the ticket inventory and sales section, which is supposed to ensure that Air Canada receives its proper revenue on tickets sold by airline sales offices, travel agents and commercial subscribers, more than 250,000 ticket sales have gone unreported. A spokesman for the union which works at the finance branch in Winnipeg has made these statements, which have gone unchallenged. Since neither the government nor Air Canada have rebutted them, I must accept them at face value as being correct. The union also said the sales were written off by Air Canada at the lowest fare charged by the airline, $25.00. This meant a loss of more than $6 million to Air Canada.
After Air Canada had experienced these huge losses as a result of a poor accounting system, what did it do? It marched down to the Canadian Transport Commission and the commission rubber-stamped a fare increase for it. Where is the protection for the public?
What are some of the other activities of the finance branch of Air Canada? Through its airline clearing house section it has paid out $40 million to other airlines without an audit, and as of September, 1975, was backlogged to October, 1973. By its failure to audit, the airline is writing off errors in billings which normally amount to $160,000 a month, or nearly $2 million in the course of a year, the union claims. Also, the union estimated that $10 million worth of coupons were still not cashed in as of September, 1975, and the backlog was as high as $20 million last year. Even if they are eventually processed, the airline will have lost millions of dollars in revenue because of the delay. Further, in press reports published in March of last year, an internal Air Canada memorandum between officials in Winnipeg and Montreal was quoted as mentioning significant delays in billing other airlines because of the processing delay.
Finally, Air Canada made a statement. A public relations officer for the corporation declared that the airline was "subject to continuous external audit procedures conducted by independent auditors appointed by the federal government", adding they were under constant scrutiny. Nothing could be

further from the truth, Mr. Speaker. They are under absolutely no scruting whatsoever.
A comptroller general will certainly have his work cut out for him. He will have to be the most competent auditor this country has ever produced. There is a mess in this country due to improper accounting which is completely out of control, and it will take many years to correct the situation. Thank heavens the government has finally taken a step forward by appointing a comptroller general.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my area of concern today will cover two topics. The first is government policy towards existing Crown corporations. Second, assuming the need for Crown corporations, I should like to discuss certain safeguards which may be necessary to ensure that government corporations pursue the goals for which they were created and that they do so under very clear rules.
Dealing with the question of whether Canada needs Crown corporations I note that at present there do not appear to be any studies done by the federal government to indicate the conditions which must exist before a Crown corporation ought to be created. There never has been, to my knowledge, any debate concerning the proliferation of Crown corporations. Perhaps it is now time to look at the underlying reasons for which a government would choose to develop Crown corporations as opposed to a system of nationalization or complete free enterprise.
It is the traditional belief that the state should intervene, or interfere with the market place, only when the market place itself cannot satisfy a given need on the part of the consumer.
In connection with Crown corporations, however, two questions are raised. First, the existence of a Crown corporation must to a certain extent mean a limitation on voluntary exchange through a reduction in the alternatives available to individuals. In the second place, the existence of a Crown corporation raises the issue of the social responsibility of that corporation since it is also an instrument of public policy. As an example of the first principle I note Premier Lougheed's statement last week that the promotion of Petrosar by the federal government had taken jobs away from Albertans. The premier maintains that Petrosar took both job opportunity and markets away from Alberta. The existence of a Crown corporation might well limit the opportunity foreseeable by private enterprise in developing certain projects.
In dealing with social responsibility of the Crown corporation, statements have been made by ministers of the Crown that Crown corporations are commercial enterprises which must operate by the same rules as most normal businesses would operate under. This may well be true, but we have never had any discussions as to whether a Crown corporation is simply a corporation operating in the private sphere of whether it is an instrument of public policy. For example I note that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) on December 16, 1976, issued guidelines for Crown corporations. In these guidelines he warned that commitment to rigorous ethical standards and dedication to propriety in business are not
April 26, 1977

without their cost. This demonstrates the dilemma which Crown corporations are facing. On the one hand they must operate according to the tough rules of business, and on the other they must exercise strict principles of ethical standards. Surely it is time that we set out plainly the objectives and goals of Crown corporations.
The rules must be made clear not only for public corporations to operate but also so that individuals in our society have a clear understanding as to the utility of public corporations. 1 am well aware of the difficulty in establishing a satisfactory objective measure as to the usefulness of Crown corporations. It is extremely difficult to decide on a set of indicators which will separate the need for private enterprise as opposed to the need for public enterprise. In fact, it would probably be true to say that no rigid set of guidelines would be suitable. The great disadvantage of either governmental regulation or governmental operation is that it is exceedingly difficult to reverse. What I am asking the government to do therefore is to initiate some form of debate as to the need for public corporations and how far a state should go in interfering with private activities.
I am not suggesting that competition alone would be an autonomous regulator of economic activity and 1 am not suggesting that all Crown corporations should cease functioning tomorrow. What I am suggesting is that the government develop some policy or national plan concerning the need for public corporations. It is unfortunate that public corporations should have sprung up piecemeal without any clear views being expressed by the government as to their exact purpose. I am asking therefore that the government articulate the rules as to the justification of public corporations. Surely governmental policy should call for a review of all Crown corporations and they should be made to justify their existence in a manner very similar to zero based budgeting.
It has been suggested by various individuals that public enterprise in Canada resulted from the small domestic markets available in this country. Surely it is time that we ask whether public enterprise is destructive and wasteful. If we are going to keep public enterprise, then we should ask what are the best ways of giving public enterprise maximum freedom from political interference without giving up ultimate parliamentary control.
Naturally, all these questions centre around the crucial question as to what is the ideal relationship between the economy and public enterprise. Perhaps we also need to look at the historical perspective beginning with the federal enterprises of the 1930's like the Bank of Canada, Polymar, Eldorado Nuclear, the National Harbours Board, Industrial Development Bank, and the second generation such as Atomic Energy of Canada, Northern Transportation, Northern Canada Power, Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporations, Canadian Patents and Developments, Petro-Canada-the list goes on. It has been estimated that Crown corporations account for over 30 per cent of all Canadian-controlled corporate assets.
Auditor General Act
There are, in addition to these, Crown corporations in cultural fields, those which act as treaty agencies, those involved in housing and urban development, and those with very specialized functions too numerous to mention. Then there is always direct government participation in private companies like Panarctic Oils and Telesat Canada. I am not suggesting that most of these enterprises have not added to cultural form in Canada. I am suggesting though that Canadian public enterprise has proliferated to a large extent without the government or the public knowing the underlying reasons behind this proliferation, and perhaps it is now time to examine some of these reasons.
The next area which logically follows from this is that, assuming we do have certain forms of public enterprise, then should we establish clear rules to enable these public enterprises to operate not only effectively and efficiently, but also under a standard which the Canadian public appreciate?
On December 16, 1976, the President of the Treasury Board disclosed in the House of Commons guidelines governing Crown corporations in relation to their commercial practices. These guidelines were generally welcomed by my party. I would point out, however, that officers and directors of Crown corporations are not at present under any higher or more rigorous standard of care and duty than that incumbent upon directors and officers of federal and provincial companies. There is not at present any statute, regulation or guidelines setting out the standard of care incumbent upon officers and directors of Crown corporations falling within the Financial Administration Act.
Truly it is now appropriate to have such guidelines or rules, especially in light of the Polysar investigation by the Public Accounts Committee. Surely it is time for the government to bring forward a proposed bill governing Crown corporations. Other areas, such as whether or not a Crown corporation should have an audit committee, would also have to be covered by such a bill. The accountability of Crown corporations, including penalties for non-observance, should be stipulated in the bill. The power to remove members of the board of directors by parliament and not by the cabinet should also be included.
These are just some of the areas which would be covered by a bill dealing with Crown corporations. The whole thrust of my argument, however, is that we do not need any more guidelines respecting Crown corporations; rather there is need for legislation and parliamentary control of Crown corporations, including their accountability. Let me close by saying that parliament must re-establish its authority over these Crown corporations in order to ensure that scandals such as Polysar and Eldorado Nuclear do not occur in the future.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief so as to fit into the available time slot. 1 welcome the opportunity of making a few short comments on Bill C-20 and I congratulate the government on the concepts included in the bill. I think the minister came into his portfolio

April 26, 1977
Auditor General Act
during a time when many matters were being discussed and this whole question was evolving. To be fair to the minister, he has certainly listened to and read many of the comments that have been made in relation to the post-expenditure auditing procedures of the government. Obviously the situation that the government faces and which most governments face today cries out for reform, and this bill is a small step along the road to reform. In congratulating the minister I certainly would not want him to be big-headed, feeling that he has found the answer for everything, because I am sure he appreciates that he has not.
The bill itself causes me some concern. I think there are some gaps in it. I am in the rather funny position that, while 1 can see the need for some amendment when the bill reaches the Public Accounts Committee, I am not so sure that 1 will be in any position to present any amendments. Therefore 1 want to take the opportunity this evening to leave the Elouse a few ideas for its consideraton, if I may.
I realize we are debating the principle of the bill and are not to engage in a clause by clause discussion, but at the very beginning of this bill 1 find a defect in that nowhere is there any requirement that the Auditor General of Canada should himself be a professionally qualified accountant. I think this is a matter that should be rectified. It may be a small thing, but I gather that there have been times in the history of the office of the Auditor General when we have had good Auditors General and bad Auditors General.
I suppose the final responsibility for choosing an Auditor General lies with the House of Commons itself, of course along with the government, but I think one of the statutory requirements of any person holding this office should be that he is licensed in Canada to be a public accountant, that is, that he should at least be professionally qualified as an auditor. I hope this small amendment can be made in the qualifications provision of the bill.
Secondly, I think the clauses pertaining to the presentation of the Auditor General's report to the House should be changed. I think it is redundant, to say the least, when the Auditor General prepares his report by December 31, or whatever is the requirement in the bill, that he should present it to the Minister of Finance who in turn tables the report in the House, and from there there has to be a reference to the Public Accounts Committee. I think these are redundant, meaningless, and unnecessary steps which should be eliminated.
There are many precedents for the tabling of reports in the House of Commons by Mr. Speaker. I think it would be, if nothing else, a symbol of the independence of the office of the Auditor General if the Auditor General's report were presented to the Speaker of the House, and the Speaker of the House were required to table it immediately. In other words, let us cut out the presentation to the Minister of Finance, who in any event has enough to do. In actual fact the Minister of Finance has very little to do with the report of the Auditor General, so my suggestion is that the report be presented to the Speaker of

the House, that it be immediately tabled, and then automatically referred to the Public Accounts Committee.
If Your Honour asks why, I would answer simply that in the past there have been abuses. The 1970 Auditor General's report was tabled on June 4, 1971. It was not referred to the Public Accounts Committee until three and a half months later, namely, on September 22, 1971. There may have been reasons for this in those days, I appreciate, but nevertheless if one wanted to, one could believe there could be a delay of 15 days before the Minister of Finance tabled the report in the House, and there could be a further delay until a Public Accounts Committee was set up. There could also be a further delay until there was a reference by the House of the report to the Public Accounts Committee.
I see no need for the intermediary of a minister, especially the Minister of Finance. I feel, on the tabling of the report by the Speaker that that should trigger off, by a statutory requirement, an automatic reference to the Public Accounts Committee, just as the tabling of the public accounts themselves should also constitute an automatic reference to the committee. This was a recommendation of the Wilson report, which is not included in the bill. 1 do not know why it was not. Perhaps the minister has a reason as to why it was not. It should be a requirement in the bill, in any event. Cut out the Minister of Finance and have the Speaker receive the report and immediately table it. That tabling should constitute an automatic reference to the Public Accounts Committee under the statutory provisions of the bill presently before us.
There are other precedents for reports to be transmitted to the Speaker and for the Speaker to table those reports. For instance the report of the Chief Electoral Officer, under the Canada Elections Act, must be transmitted to the Speaker and the Speaker must table it. The report of the representations commission, under the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, is transmitted to the Speaker of the House of Commons and the Speaker tables that report. The report of the commissioner under the Official Languages Act is transmitted to the Speaker of the House of Commons and the Speaker of the House of Commons tables that report. As a further measure for indicating the independence of the Auditor General, indicating and confirming that the Auditor General is a servant of the House of Commons, reports to the House of Commons, is not a servant of the government and does not report to the government, this bill should contain such a provision.
I note with interest, for instance, Bill 24 that is presently before the Ontario legislature requires the provincial auditor's report there to be transmitted to the Speaker of the legislature and for that report to be tabled in the House at Queen's Park by the Speaker of the legislature. That is a good move that we should follow here.
The bill should also be further amended to require that by the time the Auditor General's report is tabled the organization of the Public Accounts Committee should have been
April 26, 1977

completed. While it is not a matter that is now incorporated in the principle of this bill, it is a matter that should be so incorporated. The sooner we get the report tabled and the sooner it is referred to the Public Accounts Committee, the better the Public Accounts Committee will be able to do its job. Hopefully that is one of the reasons for this bill.
While the Public Accounts Committee is a peripheral matter to the Auditor General and the Auditor General's function, nevertheless it is an integral part of the over-all picture. Certainly the Public Accounts Committee should be organized and ready to work at the beginning of the session so that it can receive and get to work on the Auditor General's report. Therefore I think a worth-while amendment to this bill would provide, at the time the report is referred to the committee, that the committee be ready, willing and able to work. That should mean that the Public Accounts Committee is organized.
We could even sneak into this bill and put in statutory form a provision that has now been traditional in this House since the Diefenbaker days, that is, that the Public Accounts Committee should be chaired by a member of the opposition, as it is at the moment. The sooner the Public Accounts Committee is organized and the sooner the Public Accounts Committee is working, the fuller and better job it can do. Again there have been abuses of this in the past. The twenty-eighth parliament opened on May 8, 1967, but the Public Accounts Committee was not organized until one full year later, namely, May 5, 1968. That is an abuse of the whole system. This bill should guarantee that this type of circumstance will not occur again.
I hope you will forgive me, Mr. Speaker, if I refer to specific clauses, but on a bill such as this one we are looking at the over-all procedure on the matter. Clause 10 of this bill is a very worth-while provision. For the first time the Auditor General, on the request of the governor in council, is empowered to make an inquiry into any special financial matters that may be referred to the Auditor General from the governor in council. That is a very admirable clause. That is a very good innovation that, as far as I know, was not available earlier to permit the government to refer special matters to the Auditor General. There is, however, simply one defect in that, that is, I do not believe that the governor in council should be the only body that should have the power to require the Auditor General to make special inquiries. I feel that the Public Accounts Committee should also have that power. The place to make that amendment is in this bill. I would hope by the time it gets reported back to this House that there may be an amendment along that line, of course with the guarantee that any such reference would not impede the Auditor General in fulfilling his normal function.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: He can tell us that.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
He can tell us that, as my colleague points out. There are those provisions in the bill, in any event, in regard to the special requests that the governor in council can make of the Auditor General.
Auditor General Act
If we are going to make the committee system in this House work, and especially if we are going to make the most important committee of this House work, namely, the Public Accounts Committee, it should be a very special committee and have very special powers, special jurisdiction, and perhaps even special facilities. It should have the power to ask the Auditor General to make a special inquiry into matters that may concern it in relation to the post expenditure financial affairs of the government. There should be a clause similar to clause 10 permitting the Public Accounts Committee to do this.
One other matter to which I wanted to direct the attention of the House in regard to this bill is the whole question of Crown corporations, Crown agencies, joint venture corporations and institutions, and many of these quasi-government commercial operations which were unknown to the government of a few years ago. The original concept of the Financial Administration Act, as I understood it, was to make sure that government-owned, government-run, or government-controlled commercial organizations were to be audited by the Auditor General of the day. That was implicit in the original concept. Of course, things have gone far beyond that concept today.
There are all sorts of organizations in which the government has a controlling interest or in which it supervises the operation of some of these matters. I think that in any commercial operation in which the government has a substantial financial or equity position, or in which the government has the power to appoint the board of directors, there should be some close tie-in with the Auditor General of Canada.
1 am not saying that the Auditor General of Canada should audit every Crown corporation and every agency. For want of a better word, I call them Crown agencies. There are some such as Canadian National Railways and Air Canada which, I would venture to suggest, if we required the Auditor General to audit the books, it would almost immediately require a three-fold or four-fold increase in the staff of the Auditor General. Mind you, what you lose in the swings you may gain in the round-about because we pay in other ways for that auditing by an outside auditor.
In this bill there is a very serious lack regarding the whole concept of these Crown agencies. By using the term Crown agencies, I mean a much wider scope than merely Crown corporations. If outside auditors are used in any of these Crown agencies, they should report to the Auditor General of Canada. In other words, he should have supervision and direction over these outside auditors. He may not have the capacity, the facilities, or even the need to want to do the actual audit with his own staff, but he should have the direction, supervision, and control.
I believe there should be an amendment to this bill requiring that if any outside auditors are used in respect of any Crown corporation or any Crown agency, they should report to the Auditor General, who in turn should report to parliament in respect of the auditing of these matters.
5022

April 26, 1977
Auditor General Act
By Crown agencies I mean these institutions and organizations which at the moment are not technically Crown corporations, but which include organizations such as Petro-Can, the Canada Development Corporation, and other such organizations and their subsidiaries such as Polysar, the PISA group and the Polysar Europa organization. I am sure some of these subsidiaries were almost unknown to the government and the Treasury Board until some of the latest controversies occurred.
I want to say something about a matter that is not referred to in the bill but to which the minister referred very fully when he made his contribution on second reading yesterday, that is, the whole question of the comptroller general and the financial officers in the departments. I am concerned about this whole concept. I welcome the emergence and the conversion of the minister to the whole concept of the comptroller general idea. I think it is worth while. Personally I am not 100 per cent sold on the concept. I am willing to agree, however, with past Auditor General reports and past considered opinions of predecessors to the present Public Accounts Committee in which they endorsed this concept.
Certainly something has to be done in relation to governmental supervision and control and financial accountability in respect of government departments. Now that the government and the minister have endorsed this provision and indicated that it is going to be brought about, I welcome it very sincerely. However, what we are dealing with here in respect of the comptroller general and the whole idea of the financial officers is some provision whereby the people of Canada and this parliament can be ensured that the moneys voted by this parliament are used for the purposes approved by this parliament.
I can well understand the criticism the minister has received in cabinet from his cabinet colleagues, all of whom feel that they are and should be in charge of the policy decisions respecting the operations of their particular departments. Therefore the minister has gone to great pains to point out that these financial officers and the comptroller genera! will be reporting to him and not to parliament.
I can see the minister's fears. I understand them. However, as well as the accountability from the management sense and the administrative sense to him and to cabinet which are essential, nevertheless we are also talking about accountability to parliament.
As I understand my reading of the Wilson committee report, and I am referring to the report of the Independent Review Committee on the Office of the Auditor General of Canada, they noted that a number of British practices in the post expenditure review process might be usefully adopted in Canada. One of these was the appointment of specific senior departmental officials as accounting officers to relieve the ministers of some of their responsibilities. I endorse the Wilson committee's recommendation that these officers answer not only to the departmental heads, the cabinet, their own ministers and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), but that they answer as part of their duties to the Public Accounts Committee for the efficient financial administration
of their own departments, not on policy matters but financial administration matters.
I gathered from the rather vague and nebulous comments of the minister in respect of this whole matter that perhaps the matter is not completely solidified in his department. I hope the minister will take a good look at that aspect of it. Parliament has every right to know what is going on once the funds are voted. One way to ensure that disclosure is made to the public is to tie in or to tee in with these matters the Public Accounts Committee. In general, I congratulate the minister for bringing the bill forward.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-POSITION OF RETIRED CANADIAN PACIFIC EMPLOYEES-DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION OF HALL REPORT
LABOUR CONDITIONS-POSITION OF RETIRED CANADIAN PACIFIC EMPLOYEES-DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION OF HALL REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 30 I directed the following question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro):

April 26, 1977

It has to do with the implementations of the recommendations of the Hall report. Former CPR employees who retired about 19 years ago have had a pension increase of $1.50 a month since that date. I know the minister must be concerned about the terrible inflationary pressure that this puts on the economy.
I wonder if he is prepared to give them another $ 1.50 in the next 20 years. May I ask when he is going to implement the recommendations of the Hall report?
The minister sloughed off that question with a flippant answer to the effect that it is a great idea but the unions will have to be consulted on this and so will the CPR.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the unions will not object very much to some of the recommendations Mr. Justice Hall made. Let me enumerate them as follows: first, that retired employees of the CPR should be granted the same level of increase in pensions since retirement as those granted by the CNR to its retired employees. These increases have been approximately 2 per cent annually each year since 1970 and should apply to all those retired prior to January 1, 1973. These increases should also apply to those in receipt of survivor pensions.
I do not think the unions would object to the second recommendation that the provisions in the CPR pension plan terminating survivor benefits upon the remarriage of the eligible widow or widower be removed, or to the third recommendation that the provisions in the CPR pension plan requiring marriage five years prior to the death of the employee or pensioner in order to qualify for a survivor's pension be reduced to one year.
The fourth recommendation states that the provision in the CPR pension plan limiting eligibility to employees hired before age 40 be changed to read: "Hired before age 60".
The fifth recommendation is that the trusteeship of both the CPR and CNR pension plans be removed from the hands of the boards of directors of the respective companies and placed in the hands of an independent trust company. I cannot imagine any union objecting to that and I do not know why the minister sloughed off the question in that way. It was cheap on his part.
The company also does have some responsibilities, and I will be the first to admit it. The CPR has done very well in the last hundred years of its operations, and I for one would not decry the growth of that company. It has been a good thing. The company has diversified its investments. It now has investments not only in the railway but in other things such as mining, lumber, smelting, real estate, and in operations all around the world. That wealth from around the world has come not simply because of shrewd investments on the part of the company-and I give it credit for that-but also through the hard work and the sweat of loyal employees of the company. It is time to reward those employees.
I have noticed that the CPR and the CP employees are fiercely proud of their company, and I like that. I am very pleased when employees are proud of the company for which they are working. I have noticed also that the retired trainmen, the engineers, the switchmen and so forth of CPR are proud of their company and they still speak with a glow in their hearts of their relationship with that company. But these retired
Adjournment Debate
people cannot eat pride, regardless of how proud they are of their company. Somehow, they have to keep body and soul together, and a $1.50 increase in the past 19 years does not feed them very well. I would say that the company is doing itself a disservice by dragging its feet on a recommendation by Mr. Justice Hall that the pension plan be upgraded at least to the level of CNR pensions.
I just came across an article in a periodical called The Canadian Interchange, which is put out by railway men, and it notes the following:
Canadian Pacific may be better known for its railway operations, but according to a Montreal Gazette report, the company stands to earn more money from the increased use of cars over trains through its network of investments and subsidiaries.
CP owns Algoma Steel Corp. which sells material to the auto makers to build
cars.
It is a major shareholder in Dominion Bridge Co. which builds highway bridges for the cars to drive over.
It's bought into Panarctic Oils Ltd. which is looking for more oil to fuel those cars, and what Panarctic doesn't find, CP (Bermuda) Ltd.'s 25 tanker ships can bring in from oil-rich areas around the globe.
That simply underscores the fact that CP, through its global operations and all its subsidiary companies, surely has a little bit left in its accounts somewhere so that retired employees from Canadian Pacific who retired many years ago can get a little bit more out of the retirement plan than they have received to this point.
The Minister of Labour should exercise some leadership. He should bring this matter to the attention of company officials and demand that they meet the recommendations of the Hall report in this matter.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-LABRADOR LINERBOARD MILL-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON AID
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-LABRADOR LINERBOARD MILL-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question today was one of a series of questions I have directed to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) and to other members of the cabinet on the matter of the fate of the Labrador Linerboard Mill in Ste-phenville, Newfoundland, which has been in serious trouble as an industry since its establishment. The mill is probably the most modern in North America today, but it has been in serious difficulty for two reasons. The first is that the mill is too distant from the raw resource which is in Labrador, and the second is that it has been extremely difficult to break into offshore markets.
However, the problem is not as simple as I have stated and, without going into detailed reasons, it is also due to bad economic planning, of which the minister is aware. The situation has reached the stage where, as a result of drastic operating losses which had to be borne by the province of Newfoundland, the mill is threatened with closure unless, through the efforts of all concerned, the operation can be rehabilitated.
I want to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that I place no responsibility for any failure on the government opposite. Indeed my reason for being here tonight is to plead with the minister to make a determined effort to do everything within
{Mr. Olivier.]
his power to try to bring the strength of his department to bear in order to find solutions to the problems which exist. From my knowledge of the functions of his department I can say that he can provide the answers if only he shows some flexibility in the application of the objectives of his department toward the problem which exists in Newfoundland.
Unfortunately, from what I can gather, the whole, distressing story of the mill has been one of mismanagement, of decisions having been made on political rather than economic grounds. But again the time allotted to me does not allow me to elaborate on the facts which support this statement. It only allows me to say that in the pulp and paper world this mill is probably the only one threatened with closure. This is happening in an industry which is on the upturn. This, to my mind, is significant enough in itself to emphasize the dilemma which exists in my province, in that there is a lack of capability to industrialize, even given our richness in resources which we supposedly have in abundance.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I saw the seriousness of this situation last year and made the following observations to the federal government, through the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), the minister from Newfoundland, who has co-operated with me in making determined efforts to solve this problem.
I wrote the following to the minister:
To me, the basic problems are as follows:
1.	The high cost of producing a ton of linerboard, which restricts competitive capability...
2.	The difficulty in breaking into markets for linerboard. Apart from the fact that they were one of the newest mills to come on stream, they were able to operate and sell their product in 1974 and were reaching a favourable position until the 1975 year when supply overtook demand and according to I.T. & C., that was the worst year ever for linerboard sales.
3.	With ever recurring rumours of complete closure, an added problem has arisen which could force the closure and the reason is that, as a result of the uncertainty of its future, key personnel are leaving and this will mean that replacements will be difficult to find because of the same uncertainty ...
4.	As a result of the thrust of closure, there is a depressed atmosphere in the whole community ... and this is affecting the economic and social being.
5.	As a result of the lack of markets, inventory at the mill and raw resource is over a normal peak and which has resulted in continuing shut-downs, which exacerbates the state of depression.
The solutions which I shall propose this evening to the parliamentary secretary were set out in the letter, and are as follows:
1. That the federal government initiate a co-ordinated effort with the provincial government under and including the Department of Industry, Trade & Commerce, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the Department of Manpower, along with probably CIDA and the Export Development Corporation directed towards the following objectives:
(a)	to review studies carried out on the operation of the mill.
(b)	to examine ways and means of rationalizing the cost of the resource in line with availability.
(c)	to examine the possibility and the need for support funding to streamline the operation ir. order to compete with offshore capacity.
(d)	to determine the need for assistance in shipping cost to and from the mill as a result of distance from the resource as well as the distance from offshore markets.
April 26, 1977

(e)	to consider in the determination of assistance to underdeveloped countries to whom Canada provides interest free loans to establish mills, the feasibility of promoting the purchase of linerboard on the same basis .,.
(0 in the continuing efforts to establish trade with other countries that the sale of linerboard be given high priority.
(g)	to examine the possibility of finding firms that use linerboard extensively to invest in Labrador Linerboard in order to ensure capacity where those firms would provide a steady market, or alternatively to consider through Export Development Corporation, the possibility of investing in firms that use an abundance of linerboard to ensure sales, or to invest in the mill itself.
(h)	to consult with all firms producing linerboard that may have plans for expansion in line with expanding markets to invest or purchase the Labrador Linerboard mill.
(i)	that Manpower extend efforts to examine the results of high unemployment that is occurring and to examine and implement re-training and other programs, to prepare for the impending need for mobility transfers and alternative job opportunities.
(j)	that the facilities at the Harmon Base be examined to recognize the possibility of considering that base in the government's decentralization objectives, e.g., Taxation Data Centre, Canadian Coast Guard (Search and Rescue) fisheries, etc.
(k)	to investigate the physical inventory of valuable property left as a result of the phase out of the American SEAC Base and to determine its use as a result of decentralization planning.
There is still time left, Mr. Speaker. I hope the parliamentary secretary will convey my excellent suggestions to the
Adjournment Debate
minister and will secure the co-operation of all members of the government. Please remember that we are concerned about the loss of 2,100 jobs. We must try to save them, for their loss would affect the entire community in the west part of Newfoundland.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-LABRADOR LINERBOARD MILL-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the hon. member's comments and I wish to assure him, on behalf of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) and the government, that his concern is deeply felt and shared. We are all aware that the government of Newfoundland has been grappling with this problem for sometime. At this point, no commitment has been made with regard to the rehabilitation of Labrador Linerboard and the minister of DREE is not aware that a final report has been submitted by the advisory group. It would not, therefore, be appropriate at this time to prejudge the options which might present themselves in terms of the Labrador Linerboard plant.
The hon. member may be sure however, that the government will follow the progress of this matter with great care, understanding full well the crucial importance of the plant to the people and well being of Newfoundland.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.19 p.m.
